The Provisional Committee, formed on the 27th June, 1882, for the purpose of ascertaining whether by improving the Rivers Mersey and Irwell it is feasible to bring ocean-going vessels to M .nchester, presented their report to the subscribers to the guarantee fund, from whom their authority was derived. A meeting of the Guarantors was held on the 26th Septem- ber, 1882, when the ,following resolutions were unanimously adopted: 1. That the report of the Provisional Committee to this meeting be, and is hereby adopted. 2. That steps be forthwith taken by the Provisional Commit- tee to raise a fund, and to apply for Parliamentsry power to carry out the scheme as recommended in the report. 3. That so soon a., in the opinion of the Provisional Com- mit tee, an adequate fund has been raised, a further meeting be convened to appoint a permanent committee to carry out the undertaking. Copies of the reports of the engineers, Messrs. Abernethy, Leader Williams, and Fulton, together with the report of this Committee, may be had on application to the secretary. The advantages which will accrue to Manchester by raising it to the rank of a seaport cannot be better summarised than in the following words Of the late Sir William Fairburn, C.E.,

"Any improvement which will enable ocean-going vessels to discharge their cargoes in a commodious wet dock in Ilan- chester, would form an epoch of such magnitude in the history of 31ancbester as would quadruple her population and render her the first as well as the most enterprising city in Europe." There is no city in the world not situated on the seaboard or on a navigable river which has a shipping trade at all to be com- pared with that of kianehester. The proposed scheme will rescue one of the principal water- ways in the Kingdom from its present abandoned and useless condition, and by placing it in independent hands having the development of the interests of the district at heart, there will exist every guarantee for its being used as an effective instru- ment of competition, thereby cheapening the cost of transport, and promoting iucreased trade in Lancashire and the surround- ing districts. The works to be constructed will serve also to mitigate the disastrous effects of floods, will provide admirable sites for mills and workshops, and enable docks to be constructed at Warrington. Irlam, and other places, for the shipment of Lan- cashire and Yorkshire coal and goods, and, in many ways give an impetus to existing industries, and the creation of new ones.

A radius of 40 miles from Manchester includes a greater population than any similar area In the United Kingdom, the population of North-East and South-East Latcashire Mid and East Cheshire. Derbvshlre, North Staffordshire, and the West Riding of Yorkshire being in round numbers 5,500,0:-.0. Man- chester, therefore, as a e snvenient food-distributing centre has no equal in this country. It is desired to raise a fund of £lOO,OOO to meet the expenses of the application to Parliament for powers to carry out the scheme, and to which it is hoped all classes will contribute. Any subscriber will be entitled to the option of applying for twenty times the amount of his subscription in shares so soon as their issue is authorised by law. ; In the event of any subscriber not desiring to avail himself of the above option. he will, in the event of the bill becoming law, and the necessary share capital being raised, be entitled to ciaim the return of his subscript' no. It may reasonably be expected that if the proposed E hip Canal, soon after its completion, secure even one half of the shipping trade which it would have secured had Manchester been by nature a port, it will possess a revenue, after amply providing for working expenses, sufficient to pay a dividend of at least 10 per cent. on the cost of construction. From the enormous rapidity with which the shipping trade of the country is increasing, the competition of the new port in a few years will not be felt by existing ports aid carrying bodies.

The Committee appeal with every confidence to the public, and particularly to the people cf Lancashire, Yorkshire, and Cheshire, to aid in the carrying out of this important enter- prise, by signing the form of " Subscription List," which may be had un application to the Secretary. As soon as the Committee have raised a fund which they con- sider adequate, a meeting of the subscribers will be convened to appoint a permanent committee to carry out the under- taking. All communications in response to or in connection with this circular may be addressed to Mr. Henry Whitworth, Secretary, 96, King-street, Manchester.

GOOD MORROW AND FAREWELL. Pro moth i viola, pro purpurea naroisso cardnns et spinissurgit pallurns scut's.— Virgil. I had a garden once upon a time, Wherein I wandered free, Sharing hushed fragrance at the hour of prime With early bird and bee. I I loved to watch the dim, mysterious night Flit stealthily away, And listen to the chirpings of delight That hailed the dawning day. "Good morrow, to my stately lillies tall, And roses bright with dew; Good morrow, little hyssop on the wall, And laughing pansies blue I Good morrow, thistle, in the corner there, With prickles hedged about, Your friend, the finch, will soon be here to tear Your woolly gray-beard out." The salutation bath a ring of war: I loved him not at all. I longed, to root him up and fling him far Over my garden wall. But when I bade the gardener hew him down Be shook his palsied head. "Be bath his use," he answered with a frown, "And virtue, too," he said. I looked away, with scornful gesture proud, I grudged him breathing space; " 'Tis asses' provender," I said aloud, "And this is not his place." The gardener, bending with a hollow moan Unto his wonted toil, Made answer, "Where the asses hold their own Thistles will hold the soil." An odour floated towards me like a prayer From sweet-lipped suppliant sent, Then of my cream-white roses I was ware Breathed deep, and was content. For in my borders gracious things were set, Old" Honesty was there, And "Thrift," and hoary thyme, and mignonette, And " Heartsea.se " everywhere. Outside my garden wall there grew a tree Whose gloomy houghs outspread, And threw a pall of darkness ailently, Persistent overhead. Day after day more &lent grew the thade, More hurtfully it fell, And seared the dancing senbeams as they played; I said; "It is not we:i. '

And, passion-tossed, I to the gardener cried, "Cut down the hateful tree r He said, "it grows upon the neighbour's side, So ye shall let it be." His words upon my trembling, troubled heart Boomed like a funeral knell; Then, then I knew that joy and I must part, And say a long farewell. For one by one died all my pretty flowers, My heart died slowly too; "Farewell, my plea.sant, lily-haunted bowers Farewell, my pansies blue r I closed my garden door, and turned the key, Not without quiet tears; The thistles held the ground in spite of me. With all his pointed spears.
—Pr= Temple Bar._

Selow ii JULY,—The weather on July 26 will long be remembered in Melbourne for its cold bleak temperature, and the fact that snow fell in the city for the first time for about 33 years. To large numbers of the younger popula- tion of the city the sight was an unprecedented novelty, and it excited great interest in many of the schools, work being for the time, and for some time after, quite sus- pended.-31elbaurne Paper. AN ELECTRICAL SHEEP SHEARER.—According to the Colonies and India," a correspondent in New Zealand has pointed out to Mr:Edison the pressing need of some means of shearing sheep evenly, rapidly, and without risk of hurt- ing the animal, suggesting that an electrical apparatus might be omelet° answer' the cutting to be done by means of a wire highly heated by an electric current. The length of the heated wire, or cutter, would have to be about three inches. The use of an Incandescent wire of platinum for cutting has been entirely successful in surgery in removing tumours and other diseased or morbid growths, and there is a possibility that it might answer for cutting wool. A more probable method in which electricity might be employed in this direction is in the adaptation to the purpose of the cir- cular maw or rotary knife, driven by electricity, such as is employed in certain surgical operations." AN AGED EARL AND HIS AGED TENANT,—Last week, an auction was held at Snetterton Hall, near Thetford, caused by Mr. James Reeve giving up farming in favour of his son. Mr. Reeve is near 80 years of age, hale and hearty, and 'nas occupied the farm 42 years, it having been in the family 140 years; his grandfather attained 91 years. Some of the implements were very old ; one wagnon, it is said, was over 100 years. Mr. Clare Read, who presided at the luncheon, gave "the health of the landlord, the Earl of Albemarle," who, he said, was one of the Liet survivors of Waterloo. The Earl's life also embraced the first and second Egyptian wars, for Lord Albemarle was alive when Aber- cromby fell at Alexandria, and Nelson conquered at the battle of the Nile. He understood that the glorious victory of our troops this month in Egypt had kindled the en- thusiasm of the gallant old Earl, who, in common with many of his countrymen, was pleased to find that, notwithstand- ing all the scientific appliances of modern warfare, there was yet room for the display of individuel pluck and daring, and gloried that the stronghold of the rebel Egyptian was carried in true old English style, at the point of the bayonet. SUDDEN DEATH OF A HOLKER SHORTHORN.—OR Sep- tember 25 there died, at Holker, the celebrated cow Baroness Oxford, the only living daughter of Lady Oxford sth. She was perfectly well at one p.m. on Sept. 2-1. At font p.m. she was found by the herdsman in great pain, and died about six o'clock on the following morning. Baroness Ox- ford had been a vary healthy cow, and until this last illness I had never had a dam of physic. She was in her twelfth. year, a roan daughter of Duke of Claro 2nd (21,576), from Lady Oxford sth. She has bred eight living calves, and was again nearly due to calve. M. W. Bromley, veterinary surgeon, made a post-mortem examination' and found her sound in every respect. Death had arisen from inflamma- tion of the fourth stomach, and it is assumed that she must have eaten some irritant. In addition to grass, her food has been 21,1 b. of linseed cake and 21b. of crushed oats per day. Samples of the cake and oats have been sent to Dr. Voelcker for analyais. Baroness Oxford had five cow calves in suc- cession, then a bull, and afterwards two heifer calves. Baroness Oxfords 3rd and sth were sold for 3,760 gs , and Baron Oxford 9th for 1,200g5. There are five daughters -still at Holker ; also three grand-daughters and three grand- eons.—Re FATTENING ANIMALS AND FEEDING FOOR LAND.—It is the falsest economy to sell off a sheep from one of these poor light-soil lamb breeding farms. The manurial enrich- ment of such terms is everything in making them remuner- ative, and the cheapest way of manuring them is by the voidings of sheep when fed" on fattening food. Even our ancestors affirmed that these animals have golden feet; but a sheep fattened on a poor farm turns everything to gold to an extent of which they had no conception. The difference in the succeeding grain crops where turnips have been fed off in the one case by lean sheep, and in the other by those fattening and supplied liberally with artificial food, is so immense that those who have seen it will not require to have my proposition prove!. lam myself so well satisfied on the point, that on a light soil farm I would never sell off a single animal in lean condition. I would rather contract- the number bred to the capability of the farm to fatten the surplus OLIN, if it were not possible, by growing more green crops and utilising the straw as food, to effect the business without shortening the number bred. Another rearm on which I found my thesis is that the most economical method of mutton-making is that of fattening the animals from birth while they are in a state of growth, so that rear- ing and ripening for meat may proceed at one and, the same operation. The old way of converting wethers to mutton at two years old required one yeanfor the sheep to grow to maturity, and still another for fattening. It is now die. covered that the entire thing can be accomplished far better in less than one-half the time by making the fattening com- mence at the earliest age, and causing the animal to put on flesh continuously while it grOws.—Exeter Gazette. AP. SCIENTIFIC NOTES. Besex PaosPeroans. —Many chemists have doubted the existence of black phosphorus, holding that it is a mixture of ordinery phosphorus and metaltic phosphide that gives the!colonr. N. Thenard, while admitting that this may often be the case, does not think it is always so. A short time ago, when moulding phoephorus in the ordinary way, and after obtaining a dozen rods all ef the usual colour, he found that the thirteenth suddenly blackened at the moment of congealation, this effect extending throughout its mass. Other rods blackened partially. The black, or rather dark grey phosphorus becomes white again when melted, and re- mains white if cooled suddenly ; but if surfueion be pro- duced, it becomes black, as before, on contact with white or black phosphor ua. BLEACHING OF SILK.—Ia this process the silk to be bleached is dipped in a more or less concentrated solatioa of bromine, according as the colouring matter is stronger or weaker. The duration of the immersion amounts to thirty minutes. After the silk has been drained, it Is conveyed to a second bath, which consists of some dilute acid. After the expiration of about half an hoar the goods are taken out and again left to drain off. Frequently two or more bromine baths, with as many succeeding add baths, are necessary. Tartaric and citric acids furnish the beat re- sults; moreover, they can also be replaced by alkaline solu- tions, for which purpose sodium carbonate is best fitted. Sulphites and acid sulphate, as well as sulphuric acid, are likewise suitable for the second bath.—Textile Manufae-

Both replied, "Yes." "Well, then, have one another ;" and the couple were man and wife. Fist{ ACCLIMA,TIZATION.—The Norfolk and Suffolk Accli- matization Society, of which Mr. E. Birkbeck, M.P. is chair- man, have just introduced a lot of young Loch Levan trout Into the Waveney, and inbend doing the same in the upper waters and tributaries of the Yare and Bare. This species of trout is considered to be specially adapted to the Norfolk and Suffolk waters, and the experiment will be watched with great interest. The fry, which were hatched at the society's establishment at Lowestoft, and subsequently nursed at Gunton, were conveyed to their destination under the care of Mr. Oldham Chambers, the hon. secretary, and some members of the committee' at whose service Mr. H. Bullard placed hie steam launch, the party being joined on the way by the Mayor of Beccles (Mr. W. M. Crowfoot) and Mr. J. E. Crisp, as representatives of the Wavaney and Oalton Fisheries Protection Society. The young trout were deposited, part in an off-shoot and side-stream at Ellingham Mills, part at Wainford Mills, and the rest in the stream running past Mr. Norton's garden at Bangay, where it is hoped they will thrive and breed, and hold their own against the coarse fish with which the river abounds a matter of which, it is only fair to say, some persons have -ave doubts.

HOUSEHOLD PETS. Exsa.conta Dos.—lf you keep an animal it is 'imam- bent-upon you to attend to it properly, or you should not have it at all. Attention does not mean simply good food and cleanliness, all important though these may be, but as a dog requires exercise every day in order to keep its organs in a proper state, if this is neglected then it is liable to various diseases which would otherwise be entirely pre- vented. There are many people who show every possible care and attention to their pets except in this one point, and as a consequence, no matter what the breed may be, the dog gets fat and lazy, or, what is worse, offensive in its smell, and perhaps mangy. Degs that are kept confined in the kennel soon show their delight when taken out for a run, and by their actions give abundant thanks to him who liberates them. Exercise should not take place immediately after feeding time, and at least two hours ought to elapse between one and the other. The amount of exercise will de- pend upon the &ZS and kind of dog, and whilst half a mile will be enough for a sm;11 pet, four or five miles will not be too much for a large one. If one of the latter gets a two mile run every day it will take no harm, bat less than this would not be sufficient. Yard or watch dogs are often savage, and perhaps dangerous, bat as there is generally a min-servane where these are kept, it should be part of his regalar duty to give them exercise, which cart be done whilst he is going the messages. Collars As Paers.—Collies or sheep dogs have been long employed for the tending of flocks, and many are the tales told of their sagacity and faithfulness. But it is only during the last few years that they have become favourites as companions and pets. Such, however, is the case, and, although this may not be conducive to improvement so far as work is concerned, yet we know of no more pleasing house dog than a good collie. They are most intelligent, very active, are handsome when kept well and not coddled, and are neither clumsy nor yet heavy feeders. They need good but plain food, and want plenty of exercise to keep them in good order and condition. A WORD To CHILDREN.—Children are not wilfully un- kind to dumb animal', but at times unconsciously so, and we fear that loamy gets more than its share of rough usage. Whether they like it or otherwise, we are not prepared to state, but it is certainly a fact that they take all very quietly, only very seldom rebelling and giving the tormentor a scratch. We saw the other day a little fellow, jest about three years of age, carrying a kitten under his arm whilst he was outside playing, and, on inquiry, learnt that the two were never separated. Hag it and pull it about as he might the kitten always took it in good part, and if he did not take it out with him was miserable. This shows that animals are capable of affection, and teaches us the lesson that we should always be kind to them. We should try never to give pain, but always seek to do to our pussy what we should like to be done to us if we were a cat. Animals have feelings last, as we have, and understand unkindness as much as we do. HOMING PIGEONS.—Ia Belgium the keeping of Homing Pigeons is alnust universal, and pigeon racing has bean the national sport for generations. Many of the best and wealthiest citizens are members of the various clubs, and the King of the Belgtans annually offers a prize for compe- tition amongst them, besides which the Government gives a considerable amount of support to the same. In nearly all the large cities there are severel clubs, Antwerp alone possessing nearly thirty, and the admission to many of these is very difficult, indeed, to obtain, as they are kept moat select. Daring the training and raeng season the quanti- ties of birds bent away is something enormous. As the country is small, and it is found best to allow the birds to fly from the south, special trains are sent into France, where they are liberated. On one day four heavily laden trains crossed the frontier with pigeon hampers, and it was esti- mated that upwards of twenty thousand pigeons were con- tained in the same. The great prizes of the year some- times amount to thousands of pounds sterling, and the ex- citement evinced on the days of the races is very great. Truly the instinct of the birds is marvellous, which enables them to fly hundreds of miles in a few hours, over most of which they have not been before. Imams. szt THE PIGEON LoFr.—During warm_ weather, or when the loft is crowded, insects breed very rapidly, and unless something is done they will swarm all over the house and infest the birds themselves. While in this condition no animal can thrive, and the presence of these parasites is the reason why many pigeon keepers cannot succeed well with their birds. Of course the loft should be kept well white- washed and perfectly clean, in addition to which the cre- vices and joints of the perches, and corners of the nests and shelves can be washed with petroleum once a month. If the birds get insects amongst their feather., some petroleum ointment or insect powder will be found best for driving them away. GREEN FOOD FOR CANARIES.—When in a state of nature, nearly all birds are fond of green food in one form or another, but, when kept in confinement, this must be supplied to them, as they are unable to obtain it for themselves. For canaries, this may consist of lettuce, watercress, or, what is bast of all, the common groundeel. Whatever is used, let it be fresh, and, to secure its being so, it may be kept standing In water. Give freely to both old and young alike, as they will eat only as much as is good for them if it is supplied regularly; but if jot given now and again, there is always danger of them gorging themselves. ASTHMA. IN CAGE BlRDS.—Canaries are often troubled with a wheeeing in the chest, which, from its resemblance to what is known as asthma in human beings, is given the same name. It is not, however, asthma, but an affection of the lungs. The cause is not far to seek. Canaries can bear great extremes of heat and cold, delicately framed though they be, but they cannot stand sudden transition from one to the other. When they are kept in a room where the temperature is very variable, perhaps close to a draughty window during the day, with hot vitiated atmosphere from learning gas in the evening, and later on the other extreme of cold, we must not wonder if the lungs are affected. It is therefore important that care should be taken to prevent such a state of things, and this is best done by harging the cage below the middle her of the window, or, what is better, standing it on a table some distance away, and then, when the gas is light, the cage can be covered over and put on the floor in one corner of the room, as the temperature will be much more equal there than higher up. If such a plan be adopted, the so-called asthma will be prevented ; but if it is found, a little tincture of aconite is the best remedy, say a drop to a teaspoonful of water divided into two doses. FEEDING PARROTS.—Whatever may be the natural food

of parrots, that which they are accustomed to after they are captured and on the voyage to this country is maize, and as they are fond of and also thrive well on it, we think it should be made the chief article of diet. Unfortunately, however, parrots are regarded so much as pets that they are fed upon all sorts of tit-tits from the table, and as they are some- what nice in their tastes when once they get accustomed to the richer food, they begin to despise the plainer and more suitable kind. This giving of tit-bits is a great mistake, no matter what the pet may be, and it is a far greater kindness to the bird to give him that which will keep him in good health and condition than to teed him on food the tendency of which is to bring on all kinds of diseases and complaints. Occasionally a little hemp or canary seed may be given,but let it be occasionally, as parrots are very fond of these, and, if they can get them, will refuse the Indian corn. Flesh meat is far too heating, and often causes a false moult, but ripe fruit of any kind, if given judiciously, is beneficial. BUYING BIRDS.—It is a safe rule in buying birds to send to some well-known dealer for them, unless you can go and see the birds personally before purchasing. Such an one has a character to lose, and although a good price will have to be paid for a good bird, yet it is better to do this than to run the risk of being taken in. He will send what you want If you clearly state your desires, and there will be no danger of getting a worthless bird at the price of a good one. Of course, there is hardly the .ghost of a chance of securing a bargain, i.e., a bird worth twice as much as you pay for it, but this is balanced by the security from being defrauded. Above air, beware of tempting advertisementa from unknown persons, as they are generally a delusion and a snare. Reimer EIUTCHES.—Most lads have at one time or an- other kept rabbits, and for a long time only lads did so. But of late years men in good positions have not thought it beneath them to give attention to this kind of pet steer. There are many things in their favour, such as docility, i simplicity of management, and n the fact also that they take up so little room. If good hutches are provided, they can be kept in a back yard or garden, and thus a few square feet suffices for their accommodation. The first great ro- qui,ite is to have dry, comfortable hutches, and these can be cheaply made. An American bacon box can be bought for ls. or is. 31 , and if this is put in a dry piece for a few week i it will then form a very good hutch when the tpen feints are tilled up with putty. Or a new one can be very easily put together. The dimensions for a single hutch should be about three feet long, and two feet wide and high. How to make it we will describe next week. A MAN'S WALIE.—One of the most remarkable things about a man's walk is the diagonahnovement which charac• tenses it. The reader reel imagine the hands and feet to form the four corners of a parallelogram, and the diagonal limbs are of course the right arm and the left leg and the left arm and the right leg. By "diagonal movement" we therefore intend to convey the fact that the•diagonal limbs, during locomotion, always swing in the came direction. A soldier on parade keeps his arms motionless by his sides, and on no account must they ba allowed to vibrate. This is not what he would naturally do if left to himself. Watch any one person out of hundreds waleicg along the streets, and it will be seen that he invariably swings his arias as he goes along, perhaps to an extreme degree if he be a rustic, and less so if town-bred. The arms swing by the body like a eeeree of pendula, and with a speed which entirely depends upon the rate at which he may be walking. The athlete, anxtoos to complete the given nember of " laps " in a mile or con:3le o mtles and outstrip his competitors, swings his arms to and ho with a quickness which corresponds with the motion of Us swift feet; the business man also swings his arms with a motiofl which, if not so quick, exactly titritp I with the motion of his legs; and even the idle man about town, lounging along some fashionable quarter, uncon- sciously gives a slow motion to his arms which corresponds to his tardy legs. now, if the motion be even carelessly observed it will be found that the right arm swings forward at the same time as the left leg, and when the right leg is advancing it is the left arm which accompanies it. This is the natural gait, and to convince oneself that it is so it is only requisite to get a friend to walk across the room in the opposite fashion—t.e., to swing the right arm forward when I - stepping out with the right leg, and then, in the same man- ner, when bringing forward the left leg to accompany it with I the left arm. Such a gait is bath unnatural and tincomfort- ah'ee to th'-' p•ns:n whe trios it, et-el ILVIICre:I3 to tile Lb- ! server who watches a first attempt of the kind.—Science for Ali.

div.head: SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT TWELVE PERSONS INJURED.
div.p: SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT TWELVE PERSONS INJURED.

The five minutes past seven train on Monday morning from Birmingham to Sutton Coldfield, a distance of seven miles, on the London and North-Western Railway, was run into by another train whilst near the Banbury-street ticket ' platform. The guard's van and the next carriage were corn- ' pletely smashed, and the guard seriously injured. Twelve persons were hurt. For three hours traffic on the Midland Railway, British line, the London Midland Rail- way, the South London line, the North Midland line, and the other lines passing the junction was completely stopped. The exact cause of the accident is not yet known, but it is attributed to erroneous signalling, owing to the fog. The persons most seriously injured were taken to the hos- pital. Seven or eight passengers were badly injured. Donald Mackenzie, guard of the °Sutton train, was seriously injured about the head, and is in a critical state. Walter Leng, painter, Gooch-street; Benjamin Hirdstaff, labourer, South-road, Sparkbrook ; William 6immons, tobacco-pipe maker, Richmond-street, Walsall ; John Spennnch, painter, Conybere-street ; Albert Crawley, coachman, ; and John Leigh, labourer, Birmingham, were taken to the General Hospital, and aft.r being treated by the medical officers, were not detained. Official inquiries show that the five minutes past seven train from Birmingham to Sutton Coldtield was standing at the Banbury-street Junction, when, owing to some misunderstanding with regard to the signal- ling, a train from Birmingham to Leicester dashed into the rear of the Sutton train, crushing like match-boxes the guard's van and the next third-class carriage of the Sutton train.

div.p: LECTURE ON TEACIHXO FRENCH AT ST. HELENS.—On Thursday evening, a lecture was given by Professor J. D. Gaillard, of Liverpool, in which he expounded his scientific and popular method of teaching French. The lecture was given in the Congregational schoolroom, Brook•street. The Mayor presided, and, in a few opening remarks, said that i'rofessor Gaillard was well known in Liverpool and Man- chester, and he hoped the tine would come when he would be far better known in St. Helens than he was at present. He believed that Professor Gaillard's method of teaching French was a more practical and ,ffectual method than any of the alder ones, and was more speedy in making Englishmen and Englishwomen under- stand French properly, and that, of course, was the great thing. The lecturer, in the course of his remarks, mentioned that he had lived in England 20 years, and had given lectures on the subject of learning French at both Liverpool and Manchester. He then pointed out various defects in . the ordinary methods of teaching French, and referred to the necessity of adopting a more natural and subject.ive. znothcd :33 aa to 1114.n...A tlie pupil in what he WAS I,lrulUg. The lecture was an interesting one throughout, and atten- tively listened to.

FOOTBALL. • 'Cats County beat Aston Villa by two goals to ore. Darwen, after a keenly-contested game, beat Turton by goals to one. One of the Darweu men retired with his collar bone broken. In the presence of B,OOQ spectators, the Blackburn Boyers played with the Blackburn Olympic. A very fa,t and excit- ing game ended in a victory for the Rovers by four goals to one.

LATCHFORD TRUE BLUES V. ST. ANN'S RANGERS, WARRING- TON.—A match between these clubs was played on Saturday, and resulted in a " draw " in favour of the True Blues after a well contested game. Scare: True Blues, live touchdowns, one dead ball ; St. Ann's Rangers, two touchdowns, one touch-in- goal.

Dearden, the Viaduct goal-keeper, played well. WARRINGTON V. Sr. HELENS. A match was played on Saturday between the first teams of these clubs on the War- rington clubground, Sankey-street. The weather was all that could be desired, and a goodly number of spectators put in an appearance to witness the game, which was a very enjoyable one. On the call of "no side," St. Helens were the victors by one poster, three tries, and minor points (all the attempts at go sis being failures), to two touchdowns for Warrington; OiAnanieibi V. A.III.F.2TOWIf VULCAN FOUNDRY.—A match between these clubs was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors, after a very even and well-contested game. The home team had very " hard lines" in not scoring more than they did. For Vulcan J. Williams, Nicholls, and Ferguson played well; and the visitors played well all round. Score : Bt. STANLEY, LIVERPOOL (2aN TFA .s).—Tnis match was played at Haydock on Saturday last, and the weather being very fine a large number of spectators assembled to witness the game. At 4-10 p.m the visitors set the leather in motion and tried hard to work their way towards their opponents goal, but it soon became evident that their efforts were not to be crowned with the desired succes.. The Temperance men set to work and pressed their opponents hard towards their goal, where for a considerable time they had to act on the defensive in order to p-event the Haythrk team from scoring Both teams worked hard, but were unable to score before half time was called. On resuming play the ball was kicked from the eertre by one of the home team and after 25 minutes hard play a goal was secured for the Temper- ance by W. Briscoe. The remainder of the play was in the visitors' quarters, but owing to the good p'ay of the Stanley backs the home team were prevented from adding to the score. The game was a pleasant one throughout, and resulted in a victory for the Temperance by one goal to nil.

VIADUCT INSTITUTE (EARLESTOWN) V. lIA.YDOCK (ST. JAMES').---A large number of spectators mustered on the In- stitute Recreation ground, on Saturday last, to witness the opening match of the session. Owing to several players put- ting in a late appearance a start was not effected until 3-30. Luck fav aired the visitors, and they deeded to play with the wind in their favour. Hughes kicked off for the home team, and a raid was instantly made into the visitors ground, and at the very outset a tomer kick fell to the Institute players. This, however, resulted in no goal owing to the excellent back play of H H Anderton, who undoubtedly saved his goal on more than one occasion. Play afterwards became rather dull, until shortly berore half time, when Haydock scored their first and only goal. Up to this time Earlestown had been playing with ten men only. With a change of ends, and the valuable addi- tion of J Anderton, matters soon took a 111 4119 favourable'turn. and in a very short time the new comer secured the downfall of the visitors' goal. At this paint Haydock had the misfor- tttne to loso one of their men, owitig to a sight accident, which somewhat weakened their team. The Institute again scored after about 15 minutes play, J Anderton administering the final touch as the ball shot between the uprights. Most of the play afterwards took place in the Haydock quarters, and though the home platers had this advantage they failed to augmert their score. TEE "FATHER" OF THE BRITISH ARMY.—The honour °fleeing considered the "father " of the British Army is Claimed for General George Macdonald, Colonel of the Bed- fordshire Regiment, who was born on the 10th October, 4784, and therefore attained on Tuesday the patriarchal age (4 98 years. He entered the service in September, 1805, as an ensign in the 27th (In-niskilling) Regiment, which he , alnaost immediately eccompanlea on the expedition to Han- over. In 1806 he joined the army in Sicily, and was em- ployed with it until 1810, in which year he went with the 'lq3edition to Naples, and was present at the capture of ~e 4-schia and Procide. He returned to Sicily in 1811, and was etnployed there against the French Army. In 1812 he 'pro- ceeded to Spain, and was engaged at the battle of Castalla and siege of Tarragona. He embarked for Canada in 1814, and took part in the operations before Plattshurg, returning ,t?Europe in time to take part in the campaign in 1815, and the battle of Waterloo, in which crowning victory he received three wounds, namely, in the leg, in the neck, and through the body, wounding the lungs. He was Governor of Sierra ,Leone, exposed to the deadly climate of West Africa, from 4,841 to 1845, and afterwards Lieutenant-Governor of uominica, in the West Indies. He was appointed Colonel of title 16th (Bedfordshire) Regiment on the 13th February, • and attained the rank of General in the army on October 25, 1871. The great age to which this distinguished veteran has attained is the more remarkable when his wounds at Waterloo and his exposure to the malaria of Sierra Leone --that bourn from-which so few. officials ever return—rare taken into consideration.—Thaes. TRE LIBERATION SOCIETY AND ITS Wooa.—The Execu- tive Committee of the Liberation Society have issued a circular to their supporters relative to its operations during the coming season. They coregratulate them on the fact that, domestic questions are likely during the next session to receive more attention from Parliament than from excep- tional circumstances they have done in the last two sessions, and expect that new demands for reform Will exercise a • stiniulating influence on the public mind and make it pos- e, Bible to press the disestablishment question with increased earnestness. . The Society's triennial conference will be held ext May, and there will be careful preparation to render !t. effective. The number of meetings and lectures will be increased, and new efforts will be made to advance the So- ciety's principles through the medium of political clubs and Other associations. The London School Board elections Will be used as a means of urging that the surplus city • 'charities should be applied to educational instead of to •ecclesiastical purposes. There will be a renewal of agita- tion in support of Mr. Peddie's motion for the disestablish- latent of the Scotch Churn, and next session the cemetery and burials fees andlraining college questions will be dealt With. Information is being collecten relative to vicars' rates, church rates to repay borrowed money, and other ecclesiastical exactions, and also as to the proceedings of the Committee state in regard to endowed schools. The _ state that so soon as they can do so with advan- tage they will deal direcily with the, Establishment in Eng- land and Wales, and meanwhile they urge the several local c'tganisations to carry on with fresh energy a movement 'which it is stated has already made the most marked pro- grese, and will in a few more years be crowned with cora- Alete success. A suggestion that the Parcels Post should be so extended as to enable the public to send parcels through the post to any part of the world is enforced by one who has recently returned from India, who says :—" In India, whether we wish to send a parcel to an up-country town or to any place in the United Kingdom, we have only to deposit it at the nearest post-office (accompanied, in the case of a parcel for England, by a declaration of contents and value), and we have so further trouble in the matter." THE VICAR'S RATE AT COVENTRY.—The fund initiated by the Mayor a fortnight ago for the extinction of the Holy Trinity vicar's rate now amounts to £3,175, about £BOO of which has been subscribed by non-parishoners. The per- sons liable to be rated are chiefly contributing amounts equal to five years' commutation, and some members of the congregation are adding sums towards an endownment fund of £2,000 required to secure the stipend which the vicar has expressed his willingness to accept. There appears to be every probability that the sum of £5,000, fixed upon by the vestry as the amount necessary for the abolition of the rate, will be raised. EXCESSIVE PUNISHMENT AT A BOARD Scefoot : A HEAD TEACHER DISMISSED.—At the Oldham School Board on Monday night, it was reported that a head teacher at a board school had been dismissed for undue severity to a child. It was stated that the Education Department has just issued a circular to schoolinspectors urgiog them to impress on teachers and managers to avoid excesslve corporal punishment, there having been frequent complaints of such excess and its in- fliction by assistants and pupil teachers. The board expressed a strong hope that in future a birch rod will be used in its schools, and neither cane nor ruler. BoenEn EXPLOSION.—A fatal boiler explosion occurred on Monday morning at Messrs. Everitt's Kingston Works, Birmingham. Two men were killed—Henry Denston, of Herbert-road, Smallheath ; and William Mears. Frank Wilkinson, stoker's assistant, was frightfully scalded, and lies in the General Hospital in a dying state. It was very fortunate that the full staff of workmen were not engaged at the time of the explosion. Several men did not come till breakfast-time, or the consequences must have been much more serious. It is said that the boiler had to be " blown-off " a few days ago and examined. CHARGE OF PERJURY AGAINST A MAGISTRATE At Basingstoke Police Court on Tuesday, Mr. J. B. Soper, a magistrate for the borough, was charged with having com- mitted wilful and corrupt perjury on the 22nd August, in the case of a murderous assault, in which be was complainant and Mr. Arthur Croker defendant. On that occasion Mr. Soper stated on oath that, as a result of the assault, he was eonfiraed to his house for three days, and this statement, the accuracy of which was denied, formed the grounds of the present charge. After five hours' hearing the case was sent for trial to the next assizes, defendant being admitted to bail in his own recognisance and two sureties in £5O each. DESTRUCTION OP A CONCERT HALL AND HAMILTON'S PANORAMA.—Shortly after eleven o'clock on Saturday night a fire broke out at the Grand Concert Hall, West- street, Brighton, where Hamilton's Panorama has been per- forming for some weeks past. The entertainment had con- cluded and the audience dispersed before the outbreak occurred. The flames were not subdued for five hours, by which time the scenery of Hamilton's panorama and a large organ worth £2,000 were destroyed. Nothing but two side walls and iron girders were left intact. The Castle Hotel was completely gutted. The hotel and conctrt hall were insured for £14,000, but Hamilton's property was uninsured. Three policemen were seriously injured, and several firemen sustained cuts. PAINFUL SCENE AT A WEDDING.—A very painful scene was witnessed in the parish church at Sheffield, on Wednes- day. A Mr. Knowles Binns, a local solicitor and town councillor, had become acquainted, through the Matrintoniql News, with a widow named Mines, at Tunbridge Wells, who possesses the snug little fortune of £lB,OOO. Mr. Binns went to see the lady in her own house, but was • kicked out and thrashed by her brother, a gentleman named Libbert. The parties, however, continued to correspond, and yesterday they were married by the Vicar of Sheffield, after an attempt had been made to prevent the marriage by Mr. Libbert, who declared that his sister was a lunatic and that she had been confined in an asylum. The fortunate bridegroom—who re- f ueed to make any settlement on his bride—had provided himself with certificates of the sanity of the bride, and Mr. Libbert's assertion being unsupported, Canon Blakeney had no option but to proceed with the ceremony. A DANGEROUS RIDE ON THE RAILWAY.—At the Leicester Police Court on Wednesday, a man named John William Midgley was charged with travelling on the Midland Rail- way on the previous evening, without having paid his fare. On the arrival of thee Scotch express at Leicester about mid- night on the previous night prisoner was found concealed on the fore axle under the brake. He had evidently travelled in that dangerous position for a considerable dis- tance, being covered with grease and soil. He admitted having travelled in that position from Bedford to Leicester, but it was believed he had actually journeyed from London, as the train had only stopped a few minutes at Bedford. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and explained that he had resorted to the dodge because he wanted to go to Sheffield, and had no money to pay his fare. He was fined 20s. and costs, with the alternative of a fortnight's imprisonment, and went to prison in default. MESSRS. DODSON AND CAINE AND THEIR CONSTITUENTS. —Mr. Dodson and Mr. Caine addressed their constituents at Scarborough, on Wednesday evening. 'The President of the Local Government Board dealt with the Egyptian question. His desire was that Egypt should be for the Egyptians, but Arabi had as a military usurper, backed by officers who assumed the control and took charge of the army, created a military anarchy, and it was undoubtedly the duty of the Government of this country to protect at once the interests of Europeans, and more especially those of our own country- men. It Vas not the intention of the Government to remain in Egypt one single day longer than was necessary. It would be the aspiration of the Government to promote as far as the civilisation of the country would permit the estab- lishment of popular institutions in Egypt, and to restore the free and unrestricted navigation of the Canal, not for our- selves only, but for all other nations. THE S. LUXE'S MYSTERY—The charge against Franz Felix Stumm, master baker, Lever-street, St. Luke's, Lon- don, and Elizabeth Stanger, of conspiring to defraud the executors of Urban Stanger, the female prisoner's husband, who mysteriously disappeared last November, was brought up again on Wednesday, at the Worship-street Police Court. Mrs. Stanger was unable to appear, having been confines' of a child since the last examination. Mr. Poland prosecuted and Mr. Fillan defended. Charles Wintershill and Henry Coish, clerks to Messrs. Hatchet and Jones, Mark-lane, solici- tors, gave evidence respecting the endorsement and re-assign- ment of the deed of mortgage. Thomas Letch, flour factor, said the last cheque he received for goods from Mr. and Mrs. Stanger was £133 in November. Stumm had since paid him some hundreds of pounds. The name Letch on the mortgage deed was not in his handwriting.—Simon Morrell, baker, Mildmay Park, said Mrs. Stanger told him her husband had run away after ill-treating her.—Constable Unhoff, who knew Stumm in New York several years ago, said the prisoner in May made some statement about Stanger 's absence, and said he had taken possession because Stanger owed him money.—Other evidence followed, and ultimately Stumm was committed for trial, the charge against Mrs. Stanger being withdrawn. FOUR BOYS CHARGED WITH MANSLAUGHTER: EXTRA- ORDINARY AFFAIR.—The Grantham police OH Saturday were investigating a very serious affair, which has resulted in the committal of four boys on a verdict of manslaughter, by a coroner's jury. On Saturday week an aged man, named Joseph Bailey, a hairdresser, was in the act ot closing his shop when seven youths went by. Some words passed between them, and Mr. Bailey attempted to strike one of the youths with the shutter which he held in his hands. The lad put up his arm to protect himself from the blow, and what followed does not seem to be very clear. Mr. Bailey, however' fell to the ground—prabably with the shutter between his legs, and the youths thereupon made off as quickly as possible. The old man was lifted up and helped into the shop by two men who were passing, and- his wife, with the help of a chair managed to get him into the back- room, on the floor of which he lay until the next morning. Next morning he appeared to be' exceedingly ill, and a medical man was called in. On Dr. Eaton's arrival it was found that a blood vessel in the stomach had been ruptured and the thigh bone fractured. Deceased lingered until Thureday morning, when he died about five minutes past seven. On Sunday afternoon last the deceased was waited upon by the mayor, magistrates' clerk, and the chief con- stable, and his deposition taken. It appears that the deceased was not able to identify any of the youths. He would have been 84 years of age on the 27th December next, and had lived in the same house since June, 1823. An inquest was held on Friday night, and a verdict of man- slaughter was reeerded against the following boys r—Henry Panton, aged 16 years; John Huthwaite, 16 ; William Nickerson, 18; and Benjamin H. Davies, 18. The lads were committed upon the, coroner's warrant to take their trial At Lincoln Assizes. _

• nes_s, and is not allowed to see anyone. Sir Garnet WolselEy has made known his readiness to ac-) cept* the offer of a peerage. and will take his seat in the House of Lords as Baron Wolseley. In the course of Friday night the shop of Mr. White, jeweller, Parker-street, Liverpool, was entered by thieves, and goods to the value of £BOO were stolen. One of the extensive flour mills of Messrs. Baker and Sons, at Bristol, was destroyed by fire yesterday morning. The damage is estimated at from -£50,000 to £O,OOO. A man named Browne was waylaid and maltreated at Westport, on Wednesday night, by a party of men. He re- sisted, and in the struggle stabbed one of his assailants, who is now in the hospital, his life being despaired of. A police-sergeant named Waldren, who had been in the habit of going to Basingstoke station, on the South-western railway, every night, to chat with the letter-sorter of the mail train, failed, early on Thursday morning, to get off the ' carriage step quickly enough after the train had started, and was carried under the wheels and cut in two. At Middleton, 7ou Thursday, Messrs. Henry Kay and Co. were charged with a violation of the Factory Act. Mr. Hoare, factory inspector, stated that he visited defendants' silk mill on the 13th geptember, and found that a woman named Leah Stansfield had been working during the meal time, and that she had been sent out of his way into the engine-house. A fine of £3 and costs was inflicted. On Wednesday evening, while the 4 p.m. express from Limerick to Waterford was passing Cahir a stone weighing about 171 b. was thrown into a third class carriage, striking one of the passengers. A few days ago a similar outrage was perpetrated on the same line between Cahir and Tipperary, the stone on that occasion falling into a first class carriage. The trial of Edward Albert Beeton, for conspiring with Rogers, Shakespeare, and another to obtain various sums of money with intent to defraud, was brought to a close at Birmingham Quarter Sessions on Thursday night. The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour. We learn that a strict inquiry is being made at the War Office by Surgeon General Crawford, chief of the medical branch of the Army, into the reported neglect of invalids and wounded soldiers on their passage home from Egypt. It is understood that the Admiralty also intend inquiring

into the matter. On Wednesday evening a quarryman named David G-rirn- shaw was engaged at the Stanhill quarry, Oswaldtwistle, in getting some earth from beneath a large piece of rock, when the rock fell upon him precipitating him to the bottom of the quarry, which is a great depth. He was picked up life- less, his skull being fractured and his leg broken. A handsome mural tablet and bas-relief, executed by Count Gleichert to the memory of the 189 officers and men who were lost in the wreck of Her Majesty's ship Orpheus, has been erected by private subscription in the chapel at the Royal Naval College, Greenwich, and was unveiled on Mon- day afternoon. It is sta,ed that the proposed expedition to Paramatt, for identify.ng the lunatic named Cresswell, as Arthur Orton, has had to be postponed owing to the lack of funds, only £2O having been subscribed, in addition to the £lOO lodged in the Bank of Sydney by an anonymous gentleman who desires to see the last of the Tichborne case. At Clitheroe, on Thursday, three men, named Ralph Ashworth, James Cooper, and Brian Crabtree, were charged with stealing a lad named John Madden, aged 13, son of a Manchester woman. On Wednesday the boy, who is an inmate of the Clitheroe Workhouse, was seized and taken by the prisoners to a public-house, where they tried to per- suade him to go with them, but he effected his escape. The magistrates characterised the prisoners' conduct as abomin- able, but discharged them with a severe reprimand. At the quarterly meeting of the tin-plate trade, held at the Queen's Hotel, Birmingham, under the presidency of Sir Jones Jenkins, of the South Wales Works, Llanelly, re- presentatives being present from the leading establishments in the principality and the Midland districts, it was decided to advance tin-plates is. per box on the prices hitherto obtained, making ordinary coke plate 17s. per box. The last rage in Paris consists of an army of diamond "spiders " varying in size from "money-spinners "to "mam- moth spiders."' These are arranged. across the bodices of demi toilette. They begin at the left shoulder and are con- tinued across to the right side, where a large " ruby and diamond fly brooch" is fastened, the last spider seeming to be in the act of devouring the unhappy fly.—Court Jou.rrial. Selwyn College, Cambridge which has been founded "to perpetuate the noble name and labours of the late Bishop of Lichfield," was formally opened on Tuesday morning. The Master, the Hon. and Rev. A. T. Lyttelton, M.A., was installed by the Bishop of Ely. The first block of the College will accommodate sixty students, and thirty are to go into residence immediately. An important point in bankruptcy came before the Bolton magistrates, on Thursday. A publican, named Hilton, failed some time ago, it was stated in mutt with liabilities of over MAO and assets £260. The trustee, Mr. Graham, accountant, of Manchester, applied for the transfer of the license to a man named Redican. Hilton opposed this, but after argument the Bench considered that the interest of the license was vested in the trustee, who had a right to assign It, and the application for the transfer was granted. A MAN DECAPITATED ON THE RAILWAY.—On Saturday night a shocking discovery was made at Gorton. A plate- layer was walking along the railway line, and beneath a bridge found a man's head completely severed from his body. It was lying in the space between the rails of the down line, and after some searching the body was found lying between the down rails and the embankment. It was removed to the Midland Hotel, Hyde-road. The deceased, who is apparently about 50 years of age, was respectably dressed.
FORTUNE TELLERS AND THEIR DUPES.—At Waiver-

ba-m-p-io-n-,.0n Saturday, a gipsy woman, named Elizabeth Lovell (47) was convicted of obtaining sums of money and clothing by fraud from two servant girls. Prisoner told the girls she was seventh daughter of seventh virgin Jupiter, and, under the pretence of ruling the planets ad obtaining handsome husbands for them, duped them of several sums of money and clothing. Having been previously con- victea, the magistrates sent her to gaol for three months' hard labour. At Southport, on Thursday, a young man named Thomas Brown was charged with having, on the 30th ult., felo- niously wounded James Roberts with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. While the prosecutor was proceed- ing home along Kew-road, on the night of the date in ques- tion, the prisoner, without any provocation whatever, knocked him down and struck and kicked him all over the body and face. Blood issued from his nose and ears, and he became insensible. The prisoner was committed for

trial. , At Bolton, on Thursday, two men, named Thomas Smith, of Manchester, and Thomas Doyle, of Bccup, were charged with an attempted burglary. On Tuesday evening a police- man named Gillett entered the yard of the premises of Richard Sharpies, pawntroker, Halliwell-road, Belton, when he discovered the prisoners in the act of attempting to force the door from the brickwork. He seized F_inith, and Doyle ran away, but he was caught soon afterwards. There was a large quantity of jewellery on the premises. The pri- soners were committed to the sessions for trial. Information received on Thursday morning from Liver- pool states that the fine new iron steamer Highgate, 1,451 tons register, is supposed to have foundered off the Irish coast, and it is feared all her crew have perished. The vessel left Liverpool for Hamburg on the 30th September, with a valuable,cargo of goods, and would encounter the storm of last Sunday week in full force. Since she sailed from the Mersey nothing has been seen or heard of her and all hopes as to her safety are given up. A large meeting of colliers in the employ of the Bowling Iron Company was held on Wednesday, at Dudley Hill, Bradford, to take into consideration what action should be taken with reference to the miners on strike at Cleckbeaton Colliery. The men on strike were tenable to regain their old price, but it was to prevent a general reduction that they applied to the, whole of the miners to help them. They wished to do away with bye-work, which was stated to be a reduction of 20 per cent. It was resolved that all miners in two dozen pits belonging to the company, would strike in a fornight, if the men at the Cleckheaton Colliery did not have the old price of 4s. Bd. per ton restored to them, and a general advance of 15 per cent. upon the present rate of wages. The Channel Tunnel correspondence was issued on Thursday. The conclusion arrived at by the Channel Tunnel Defence Committee is that it would be presumption to place absolute reliance upon even the most comprehensive arrange- ments with a view of rendering the tunnel "absolutely use- less to an enemy in every imaginable contingency." The Duke of Cambridge at the close of a long memorandum says be feels it to be his solemn duty to warn Her Majesty's Government of the great risk and danger which will be en- tailed upon this country by permitting under any circum stances, and even though all precautions have been taken, any tunnel constructed. Sir J. Adye thinks that the Corn mittee's recommendrtions both as to defence and closure will amply suffice for the objects in view, while Sir G. Wolseley is of opinion that the hour when the tunnel is sanctioned will be a disastrous one for England. lugestre Hall, one of the seats of the Earl of Shrewsbury, Premier Earl of England, was destroyed by fire on Thursday morning. Between two and three o'clock, fire broke out in one of the upper rooms of the hall. Information was at once sent to Stafford for the county fire engines which started without delay to Ingestre. Meanwhile Lord Shrewsbury's private engine was brought to bear upon the flames, but without in any way checking their progress. The domestics and other servants on the estate ,were engaged in removing the furniture and valuable paintings and heirlooms of the family, a considerable portion of which was saved. On the arrival of the Stafford engines a large volume of water was thrown on various points of the burning building ; but, notwithstanding the utmost exertions, the firemen were unable to obtain the mastery of the fire, and the fine hall was entirely destroyed. Only the bare walls remain standing. The Earl and Countess are at Alton Towers.—Another correspondent, who describes In- gestre Hall as the most picturesque Elizabethan mansion in England, telegraphs :—The fire originated in a state bed- room, and, as only three servants were in the house, was not discovered till five a.m. Before steam fire engines could be summoned the flames bad spread with fearful rapidity, leav- ing barely time to save the chief of the magnificent pictures and other works of art. Efforts to save the building were useless, and by nine or 10 o'clock nearly all the mullioned bay windows fell out and the walls began to fall down. The grand historical oak staircase is destroyed. The damage amounts to over £lOO,OOO. The place is insured in the Guardian Office. Lord and Lady Shrewsbury were to come in for the winter in a day or two. The interior walls were hal f-titnbered, and but little time was required, to gut the • place,
