ait GARNET WOLSELEY'S DESCRIPTION OF THE BATfLE OF TEL-EL-KEBIR. Sir Gernet Wolseley's despatch describing the battle of Tel-el-Kebir, appeared in the Lon:lon Gazette of Friday. It is dated Cairo, September 16th. Sir Garnet says he has already telegraphed the result of the battle, in which he completely defeated the enemy with very heavy loss, cap- turing 59 field guns, vast quantities of ammunition, mili- tary stores, and supplies of all sorts. "Major-General Drury-Lowe was ordered to push on with all possible speed to Cairo, as I was still most anxious," continues the general, "to save that city from the fate which befel Alexindria in July last. The cavalry marched 65 miles in two days. The garrison at Cairo—about 10,000 men—laid down their arms, and our troops took possession of the citadel. A message was sent to Arabi Pasha, through the Prefect of the City, calling upon him to surrender foithwith, which he did un- conditionally. He was accompanied by Toulba Pasha, who was also one of the leading rebels in arms against the Khe- dive. The result of the battle of Tel-el-Kebir has been the entire collapse of the rebellion. "I am able," says Sir Garnet, "to report the war to be at an end, and that the obiect for which this portion of Her Majesty's army was sent to Egypt has been fully accomplished." The General then proceeds to narrate the events of the three days in detail. From the daily reconnaissance of the enemy's position, and from information obtained from spies and prisoners, he believed that Arabi had 60 guns, two in- fantry divisions of about 20,000 men, three regiments of cavalry, about 6,000 Bedouins and irregulars, besides a force of 5,000 men, with 24 guns at Salahiyeh. Against these Sir Garnet could only place in line about 11,000 bayonets, 2,000 sebres, and 60 field guns. The enemy's position was a strong one and to have marched over the intervening plateau by daylight would have entailed enormous loss. Sir Garnet wished to make the battle a final one, and to fight the enemy decisively in the open desert. The cultivated country was practically impassable to a regular army, being irrigated and cut up in every direction by deep canals. Sir Garnet having given an outline of the battle such as has been already described by telegraph, says:—"All the previous actions had been chiefly cavalry and artillery affairs, but this was essentially an infantry battle. Ido not believe (he adds) that at any previous period of our mili- tary history has the British infantry distinguished itself more than upon this occasion. I have heard it said of our present infantry regiments that the men are too young, and their training for manceuvring and fighting and their powers of endurance are not sufficient for the requirements of modern war. After a trial of an exceptionally severe kind, both in movement and in attack, I can say emphatically that I never wish to have under my orders better infantry battalions than those whom I am proud to have commanded at Tel-el-K ebir." Our casualties have been numerous, but not so many as Sir Garnet had anticipated. He adds :—lt would be impossible, in this despatch, to bring under notice all the services worthy of mention; but I must specially refer to General Sir John Mye, Lieut.-Generals Willis and Hamley, Major- Generals Sir A. Alison, the Duke of Connaught, Drury- Lowe, Macpherson, and Graham; Brigadier-Generals Good- enough, Sir Baker Russell, and Dormier ; and Deputy- Adjutant Tanner, Col. Ashburnham, and Capt. Fitzroy, who commanded the Naval Brigade. The medical arrangements were all they should have been, and reflect the highest credit upon Surgeon-GeneraL Hanbury. COMPLETE TRANQUILITY. Rhin Pasha has issued a statement announcing that com- plete tranquility prevails throughout the country, and that the state of puLlic security is perfectly satisfactory. It does not appear that the Egyptian Minister has taken a too sanguine view of affairs, for all recent accounts from inde- pendent sources indicate that Egypt is fast returning to her old patient, plodding ways, and that the last sparks of in- subordination have died out under the very forcible treatment of Sir Garnet IVolseley. SULTAN PASHA'S VIEWS OF THE SITUATION IN EGYPT. A special correspondent in Cairo sends the substance of the views of Sultan Pasha, the President of the Chamber, on the situation in Egypt. Sultan Pasha thinks that Turkish intervention in any form would mean anarchy. The sections of the population in which free educated opinion exists are strongly opposed to the intervention of any other power than England. Sultan Pasha, while accepting the control maintains that its cost is extravagant, and that £400,000 might be saved annually for the substitution of efficient natives for Europeans, and the abolition of unneces- sary posts. He admitted that the mass of the population was wholly unfit for representative government, but main- tained that there were very ntimerous and increasing classes fully deserving to be entrusted with the duty of electing members to a free Parliament. FAIR PLAY FOR THE TURK. The Porte has proposed an internal reform for Turkey, which seems only fair and just. Hitherto, foreigners en- gaged in any business or profession in the empire have been exempt from direct taxation. In Egypt, it will be remem- bered, this privilege constituted one of the most substantial complaints of the genuine National party. Now the Porte points out that this exemption places foreigners at an undue advantage in competition with natives who pay taxes, and proposes to levy a license charge upon all such persons. Several of the Great Powers have given a conditional con- sent to the proposal, stipulating, however, that Europe shall have a right of revising the tax at the end of three years. The Turk is a great nuisance to all his neighbours, and does not deserve much consideration at their hands. He has, however, a right to fair play both abroad and at home, and this reform—at first sight. at any rate—only seems to secure him that fair play. EXECUTIONS AT ALEXANDRIA. Hadji Mustapha, the water-seller, was hanged at Alexan- dria on Saturday for rioting on June 11 and killing Europeans. Large crowds of the foreign inhabitants as- sembled to witness the execution. Ladies in carriages were also present. On Monday morning the murderers of Dr. Ribton and M. Cattani were hanged at Alexandria. No disturbance occurred, though no British troops were present. These executions, a correspondent says, are becoming one of the regnlar sights of Alexandria. It is cnly to be hoped, he adds, that the evidence against the prisoners is tolerably truthful. ENGLAND AND TURKEY. The reply of the British Ambassador to the Turkish Note on the evacuation of Egypt informs the Sultan that Her Majesty's Government desire to withdraw their forces as soon as may be. But a portion'of the army must be retained until tranquillity is re-established in order that the sacri- fices which England has made may not be nullified. Turkey, it is said, is not quite satisfied with Lord Dufferin's reply. The professions of friendship and the announcement that a portion of the army has already left are well enough, but the declaration that some soldiers must remain until order is thoroughly restored is considered too vague, and the Porte threatens to appeal to the Powers on the subject. ARABI PASHA. A correspondent telegraphs from Cairo that Arabi's life is far from safe. "Such incidents," he says. "as the remark of a member of the Khedive's entourage that he would like to administer to the arch-rebel a cup of bad coffee, or the Khedive's remark, Arabi and I cannot live in the same country,' or Riaz Pasha's to a similar effect, might demoralise the Circassian savages guarding the prisoner." The correspondent declares, moreover, that Arabi's treat- ment is unnecessarily harsh, and that he is placed on the footing of a condemned convict before his trial. Meanwhile the indictment of the rebels has been drawn up. It charges them with having instigated and taken part in the June massacres; with having directed the burning of Alexan- dria, and with having abused the flag of truce. The British Government has, it is stated, been furnished with a draught of the indictment, and been advised of the course of pro- cedure. Another correspondent says he has been assured on excellent authority that no genuine documents establishing the complicity of Arabi in the outrages at Alexandria have yet been discovered. A third correspondent says that up to this moment the preliminary inquiries all tend to support Arabi's assertion that the outrages were committed against his will. The representative of the Standard, who certainly cannot tio. accused of a tendency to sentimental exaggeration, declares that last Saturday night one of the chief Palace eunuchs, with several armed men, entered Arabi's cell, roused him up, spat on him, and treated him with such violence that for some time his life was in danger. Several Palace officials are accused of complicity in this scandalous outrage. The friends of Arabi in this country—Mr. Wilfred Blunt at their head—have employed the Hon. Mark Napier to attend as counsel for the ex-Dictator at his approaching trial. Riaz Pasha has informed Mr. Napier that he will confer with Sir E. Malet on the question of permitting him to appear for the defence of the imprisoned Pasha. THE HOLY CARPET. An accident is reported to have happened to the Holy Carpet. The Canopy under which it was placed was caught by a telegraph wire during the journey to Suez, and the sacred emblem was exposed to view. At present there is some uncertainty whether another ceremony will not have to be performed at Cairo. Dr. Beag, preaching in Edinburgh on Sunday, said that in doing homage to the Holy Carpet the British Army had been called upon to practice one of the grossest forms of idolatry in the world. It was a fearful injustice to the soldiers of Britain that they should be required to do a thing so degrading as that, and the British Government and people were responsible unless they disowned the act. MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS. A despatch from Cairo states that a considerable number of Frenchmen who held positions under the Control have returnea to the cap'eal, and expect to be reinstated in their former posts. The Duke of Connaught, who is making a short journey in the previously disturbed districts, has been extremely well received by the people, who have thronged to see him at the railway stations, and illuminated their towns in his honeur. Our soldiers in Egypt should at last be happy. Sir Nathaniel Rothschild with splendid generosity has sent them a present consisting of fifteen tons of tobacco and 15,000 pipes. Sir Garnet has ordered the immediate distri- bution of this little gift, and a cloud ought speedily to arise in Egypt such as will hide the tops of the Pyramids and fairly dim the splendour of the eastern sun. Major W. A. Fitzgeorga, 20th Hussars, the bearer of Sir Garnet Wolseley's despatches announcing the victory of Tel- el-Kebir, is not to receive the money grant of £5OO which has hitherto been given to the officer who has brought home the news of the close of a campaign. Major Fitzgeorge will, however, obtain a Brevet Lieutenant Colonel for his services, and also, it is believed, a Companionship of the Bath, for having acted as private secretary to Sir Garnet Woleeley throughout the recent operations.—Standard.

Sir Garnet Wolseley and Staff are expected to leave Cairo about the 21st inst. Sultan Pasba has been rewarded for bis loyalty, accord- ing to 'e telegram from Cairo, by a gift of ten thousand livres from the Egyptian TreAsury. It is stated in a Paris journal that the French Govern- ment would undoubtedly be unable to give its assent to the abolition, pure and simple, of the Joint Control in Egypt. Troops are arriving steadily at Alexandria for the re- turn voyage to England. General Drury-Lowe embarked there on Saturday with the staff of the Cavalry Division. There is a report in Constantinople that the Sultan con- templates depriving Baker Pasha of his rank and decorations, in consequence of his having left Turkey without permis- sion. _ . .

Cotton, says a correspondent at Alexandria, is now coming in freely at Massourah, and full prices are being realised. It is estimated that the crop will be about 25 per cent. below the average. A Geneva Correspondent telegraphs that recruiting for the Egyptian gendarmerie is still going on at Berne, but that the Federal Council will probably forbid further enrol- ments as constituting a breach of international law. The trial of Arabi and his chief supporters opens to-day (Saturday). The following will be arraigned with their leader: Toulba All, Fehmy Abdelal, Samy Toulbe Yakoob, Mahmcud Femhy, Omau Rahmy, Ali Rouby, and Said Kandil. A nominal list of the prisoners awaiting trial by court martial has been handed to Sir Edward Male. It contain 113 names, but this number is exclusive of the prisoners in the provinces. The list of the latter has not been received, but it is stated by the Egyptian Government not to exceed 30 names. _

According to various telegrams, while Sir Auckland Colvin, who is now on his way to Egypt, has been in- structed not to resume his functions as Comptroller, M. Bredif, his late French colleague, has been relieved of his post altogether. Considerable satisfaction, it would appear, has been created amongst the English troops in Egypt by the announcement that all officers of the rank of major-general and upwards are to be decorated with the Osmanieh •, all other officers with the Medjidieh ; while the rank-and-file receive a medal. From Alexandria we learn that the Sheik who was arrested two days ago at Tantah for attempting to stir up the native population against the Europeans has received 100 lashes, and will be kept in confinement. Large quantities of arms have bden seized at Tantah, and the number of watchmen his been doubled. .

An address has been presented by the Governor and in- habitants of Ismailia to General Sir Owen Lanyon, thanking him, as a commander of the town, for his cordial co-opera- tion with the civic authorities, and for the maintenance of order. Sir Owen has received from the Khedive the Third Class of the Order of the Osmanieh. A Berlin Correspondent telegraphs that the negotiations between England and Turkey with reference to the Egyp- tian Question are proceeding very slowly. . The Powers are not anxious to have things hurried, as the present state of affairs in Egypt is not considered dangerous to European peace or to the tranquility of Egypt itself. It is stated that on the prisoners, numbering about 130. being delivered up to the Egyptian authorities, the British Government made it an absolute condition that they should be allowed legal assistance. The Egyptian Government contends that it is not bound by this stipulation to permit foreign council to be engaged, unless the British Govern- ment insists upon it. As indications of the damage done to Egyptian commerce by the rebellion, a correspondent at Alexandria sends a few interesting fizures. He states, for example, that from Sep- tember 1 to the present date the arrivals of cotton have been 2,000 cantors, against 110,000 during the same period of 1881. The statistics of other articles are equally

striking. About 115 persons have been arrested in connection with the outrages at Tantah, and the trial of these has already be- gun. There still seems a good deal of excitement in the palace, as the Notables have requested that the British troops should remain there for the present. A similar request has been forwarded from other places in the in-

tenor. It is officially confirmed that Major-General Sir A. Alison has been appointed to the chief command of the army of occupation. It is almost certain that Major-General Harman will command the troops stationed at Alexandria, and that General Graham will remain in command of the second brigade. The future commander of the fourth brigade is not yet known, nor has anything transpired at headquarters concerning the definite composition of the British headquar- ters staff.

Complaint is made in California that, while the judges of the superior courts get salaries of £BOO, the official short- hand writers frequently make £2,000 a year. On Saturday morning a large hardware factory in Paris was burnt down. Lieutenant-Colonel Froidevaux, one of the chiefs of the fire brigade, was killed whilst gallantly encouraging his men. A telegram from Maritzburg .announces that General (" Chinese ") Gordon has resigned his post in Cape Colony in consequence of a disagreement with the Ministry as to the policy to be adopted in Basutoland. The official liquidator of the Union Generale has com- menced proceedings against former directors and officers, with the purpose of compelling them to provide a sum of 20,000,0001.V0r the benefit of the creditors. M. Tisza, the Hungarian Premier, being interrogated in the Diet as to the ground on which he bad proclaimed the state of seige in Pressburg,where the "village ruffians" have been plundering and murdering the Jews, energetically re- plied that he should protect honest citizens by all the nseans in his power without regard to the personalsonvenience of cut-throats. ASSAS6INATION OF A RUSSIAN GOVERNOR.— The St. Petersburg correspondent of the Daily Telegraph states that news has been received there tthat the Governor of the Jabaukaiski District, in Eastern Siberia has been murdered. He was shot dead with a pistol by a female political pri- soner. It seems the mines of Nortscheusk and other penal settlements, where numbers of political prisoners are con- fined, were under the administration of this governor, and that the tragedy took place at Ichita, the administrative centre of the district. The elections in the United States have opened with a re- markable success for the Democrats. The great State of Ohio has pronounced in favour of the Democratic "ticket" by a majority which is fixed as high as 15,000. The re- presentation of the State in Congress will be "about reversed." The defeat of the Republicans in Ohio may and probably will have disastrous consequences for the same party in New York and other States. The Republican leaders were confident of succeeding in Ohio, although they knew that they should lose the votes of the Germans, who are offended at the attempt to carry out the Sunday closing law and the prospect of the introduction of a prohibitory liquor bill. It is now seen, however, that the opposition to prohibitory legislation is stronger than had been expected, and Ohio is in consequence handed over to the Democrats. THE COMING ELECTIONS IN ITALY.—The Italian Prime Minister, Signor Depretis, speaking at a banquet at StrAdella, on Sunday, defined the Ministerial position in view of the coming elections. He described the great work which hau been accomplished by the Ministry—the reform of the electoral method—and proceeded to reply to criticisms passed upon his policy. The cry raised by the Opposition for increased armaments he. strongly deprecated, pointing out that such increase was totally unnecessary and, in fact, impossible, in view of the present condition of the Budget. Italy's relations with all the Powers were quite friendly, and, continued the Prime Minister, "our relations with England, our ancient and sure friend, are excellent. Docu- ments, which will be laid before Parliament, will show that our acceptance of the invitation to intervene in Egypt wsuld not have been consistent with our international duties." A QUESTIONABLE CANDIDATE.—SOMe excitement was created in the town of Lancaster, South Carolina, a few days ago by the unwarrantable conduct of a number of negroes at an election meeting. The notorious "Colonel Cash," who, as the correspondent of the Nem _York Times plainly puts it, "murdered Colonel Shannon in a duel" in 1880, is now soliciting election to Congress as an Independent candidate. He addressed a meeting at Lancaster Court House, and as a matter of course a " difficulty " followed, and pistol shots were exchanged by zealous partisans in the crowd. Subse- quently a number of negroes, "mounted on mules and horses and armed with pistols," rode through the streets, and the fusillade recommenced. A coloured gentleman named Crockett, who led the procession, received three bullets in his chest, and fell dead, and three of his com- panions shared his fate, whilst six others fell wounded from their horses or mules. The survivors decamped with all speed, and a survey of the field of battle showed that no white man had been even scratched. Nevertheless, it was thought necessary to telegraph to the Governor of the State for troops "to suppress a negro riot," and the militia would have been called out had not a later despatch informed the Executive that "order had been restored." The Indepen- dent candidate must have derived much enjoyment from the day's proceedings.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The North Staffordshire coalowners on Monday acceded I to the application of their miners for an advance of 10 per cent. in wages. About 20,000 men are concerned. The North Wales miners are again about to demand another increase in wages. A conference of the miners representatives has been held, and it was resolved to give notice for a further advance of 15. per cent., the notice terminating on November Ist. The miners contended that, notwithstanding the advance of 5 per cent., conceded by the coal owners a fortnight ago, their rate of wages are still con- siderably below those of the Lancashire and other coal- fields. BILLS OF SALE AND FAILFRES.—In the week ending October 7, 1882, there were 81.6 bills of sale in England and Wales a decrease of 219 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 194, an increase of' three. The totals for portion of year to October 7, 1882, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 36,294, a decrease of 2,446; the failures gazetted number 8,144, a decrease of 754.—Stabb's Mercantile Ga:ette. On Saturday the accountant's certificates regulating the wages of the men employed in the Cleveland ironstone mines and the blast furnacemen employed at the Cleveland blast furnaces were issued. They show that the average I price of No. 3 Cleveland pig iron for the past three months has been 435. 2-04 d. This will advance the wages of the men 1i per cent, WAGF.i IN THE EAUTHERWARE TRADE.—The china and earthenware manufacturers of the Staffordshire Potteries decided at Hanley, on Monday, that the rules of the opera- tives for the re-establishment of the arbitration board would undermine the basis upon which the trade had hitherto been Ilcarried on. They also decided that no increase of wages could at present be given, and that the rules had been sub- mitted too late for the board to be formed in time to affect I next year's arrangement. The nailers of South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire determined on Saturday to form an Anti-Truck League. Many persons will learn with astonishment that although the old truck system has been abolished in the district, Ifystematic pressure is still brought to bear upon the workers, who are compelled to use "truck" shops and pay unreasonable prices for their provisions. It was stated at the meeting on Saturday that this system of intimidation affects nearly 60,000 people. WAGES IN THE COAL TRADE.—The question of the hour at present, says "The Engineer," is the demand of the miners for 15 per cent. advance in wages. An important meeting of coal owners has been held at Sheffield, when the resolutions of the men were under discussion. The principal resolution, which states concisely the whole question from the employers' point of view, was as follows :—That there has been no advance in the price of coal to warrant any ad- vance in the wages of the miners; but with a view to settle the question of wages upon a permanent footing, the masters are willirg to renew the offer made in 1881, and to take as a basis for the regalation of wages the net average selling price over the last two years ending June 30th, 1882, or any one of the four half-years as may be selected by the workmen • and to give the miners the earliest possible ad- vantage of any`rise in the price of coal, they are willing to submit their books at once to the inspection of competent 'accountants to be appointed for the purpose, with instruc- tions to ascertain the net selling price for the three months ended 30th September, 1882." THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark Lane Express says :—" During the past week the tempera- ture has on the whole been higher, and- an electrical con- dition of the atmosphere has prevailed. Some storms have occurred, but for the most part the weather has been fine, and good preparation has been made for wheat-sowing, which has commenced favourably. There has been no improvement to note in respect of the condition in which the offerings of native wheat are now put forward, and the supply has been rather irregularly distributed. In London, on Friday, an unsuccessful attempt was made to improve on the rates current on Monday last, but in several country markets on Saturday selected samples of English wheat realised is. per quarter more money. Country flour is weighed down by large arrivals of foreign brands, and in London the trade has ruled very dull at the decline noted on Monday last. The supply of fine samples of malting lbarley is restricted, and values tend upwards; but for !English grinding barley there has been no change to note. All descriptions of new oats are in the buyers' favour. Beans and peas unchanged. Trade for foreign wheat off stands in London has been marked by a hard struggle on the part of sellers to effect a general improvement in value ; but the success has not been great, and at best but partial. THE LANCASHIRE COIL TRADE: MANCHESTER, WEDNES- DAY.—The pressure of orders which came in during the close of last month is being gradually worked off, and where colliery proprietors are still pushed it is more with the com- pletion of deliveries on account of old orders than with new business coming in. All classes of coal are, however, going off very freely. The pits are kept on full time as much as possible, and at most of the collieries in the Manchester dis- trict the full average output is being raised, but in the West Lancashire district there seems to be an almost general de- termination amongst the men to restrict the get, which at many of the collieries is not at present reaching more than about two-thirds the average quantity. Prices continue firm at the advanced rates. The average prices at the pit mouth are about as under :—Best coal, las ; seconds, 7s 61 te 8s 61; common house coal,. 6s 61 to 7s; steam and forge coal, 5s 9d to 63 3d; burgv, 4s 9,1 to 5s 31; ordinary slack. 3s 3d to 3s 9d, with special qualities in some cases quoted up to 4s CI and 4s 9i per ton. A good business is being done for shipment at prices about is 6d per ton above the lowest point. Delivered at the high level, Liverpool, or at the Garston docks steam coal averages 8s to 8s 6d, seconds house coal Os to 9s 6d, and better qualities us to us 6d per ton.

div.head: LORD DERBY ON THE CRIMINAL CLASSES.
div.p: LORD DERBY ON THE CRIMINAL CLASSES.

The Earl of Derby took the chair on Monday at the I annual meeting of the Manchester and Salford Discharged Prisoners' Aid Society, held in the Town Hall, Manchester. In moving the adoption of the report his lordship said the case for discharged prisoners' aid societies was simple and, he thought, unanswerable. The condition of English life made it difficult for discharged prisoners to get employment, but in a new country, where the demand for labour was always, or almost always, largely in excess of the supply, the difficulty would not arise. But in this old and crowded country it was not always easy fora man who had got HO character, or, rather who had got a character very much to his disadvantage, to find work, even if he had what is called a trade in his fingers. Amongst the educated and civilised workingmen there was a natural and honourable feeling—a feeling which he did not in the slightest degree blame— which made them reluctant—as men in other ranks of life would be reluctant—to associate with men who had got into public disgrace. It was easy to say " It's their own fault ; it's quite right that they should suffer ; let them alone." But they wouldn't let other people alone. It was easy to talk about rascals and gaol birds not being entitled to sympathy. For his part he did not profess any particu- lar sympathy for them, but he had a very strong sympathy for the honest 'part of the community,'on whom and at whose expense they would live if they could not get a living in any other way. They could not do with them as they then did with wasps—take their nests and destroy them. What they had to do was to see if some at least of these human wasps could not by proper management be turned into bees. (Hear, hear.) There were many persons who thought that criminals as a body were an irreclaimable class, and that any trouble taken for them was only trying to wash negroes white; but that was too creeping a generalisation, and it was not one borne out by facts. There were those who came under the law—various and distinct types of character ; there were those who had been brought up by dishonest parents, or had been turned loose into the streets in their childhood, and had never had the choice between good and evil placed before them, and unless they were lucky enough to be caught young and sent to a reformatory or an indus- trial school, there was scarcely a possibility of their conduct- ing themselves in an orderly and honest manner. These were not incurable if they could be got hold of. Then there was another class also who were weak, rather than deliber- ately perverse. These were reclaimable. There was a third class who were morally worse than either of the others, but yet one which he should not consider as hopeless. He meant those who - had more brains than the average offenders who came before the courts of law. They were an exception, he admitted, for the feature about the criminal class which had struck him most was their extraordinary and exceptional stupidity. Then there was the large class of casual offenders as dis- tinguished from habitual offenders. No doubt, when allowance had been made for all these, there did remain an irreclaimable residiam. There were natures which appeared utterly perverse, and individuals who had a deliberate preference for crime. For thvn there was no hope so far as one could see, but they were a fraction of I the whole. They must, of course, be on their guard against patronising offenders, and against doing anything to put them in a better condition than those of their own class who had not fallen into bad ways. He did not think there was much tendency in that direction. There were two things they wanted the public to remember. One was that whatever our prisoners might be like we had got to keep them with us; the other was that by offering shelter and work to every discharged prisoner who wanted it, they took away what was the favourite excuse of the really irreclaimable convict. Such a man stood in the dock acid said : "I did not want to go wrong again, but nobody would employ me ; nobody would give me a chance." Very often—probably in the majority of cases—that statement was a lie. Sometimes, no doubt, it was true, but whether it was true or whether it was false, in the interests of justice it was a good thing to be able to refute it, and they could refute it if they could say to such a man : " There is a Prisoners' Aid Society ‘vhich would have taken charge of you; why did you not go to it?"

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 14, 1882. -

IF we may judge by the utterances of Tory orators during the past few days, the coming autumn session of Parliament will be a lively one. The object of the session, as we are all aware, is to so revise the rules of procedure in the House of Commons that obstruction may be effectually checked, waste of time avoided, and that Parliament may have some control over its business, which it certainly has not under existing conditions ; but of course it is the intention of the Government that other pressing questions shall receive attention, and inde.,l if that were not so, we receive ample evidence day by day that the Opposi- tion would not be satisfied. lii every quarter almost of the three kingdoms Conservativ3 mernbers are holding forth nightly to appreciative as well as un- appreciative audiences ; and we may be sure that their misleading and unguarded statements will be repeated within the walls of St. Stephen's at the very first opportunity. The brunt of the attack is being sustained by the legal luminaries of the Oppo- sition, for the reason, we presume, that their training better qualifies them for gulling audiences than that of some of their less-favoured colleagues ; but at the same time the efforts of Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett—who takes the Eastern question under his especial protee- tion—and other minor lights, serve a_useful purpose if

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 14, 180.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 14, 180.

( only to 'mow that there is some vitality in the Fourth 'a its leader is still silent. Mr. Gibson, the Party, thong, al for Ireland in the late Administra- Attorney - Genet, —Giffard, the Solicitor-General tion ; Sir. Haeuiggeeconsfield's Government ; for England in Lord is.. ets to succeed Sir and Mr. E. Clarke, Whe°?4'. in the Sails- Hardinge Giffard as SolicitorsOeMme. -ming in bury-Northeote Administration whc tn. the future, have been addressing audieneeta )-_ cheater and Galashiels, at Launceston, and at Dara lington, respectively; and a perusal of their- speeches will impel any impartial critic to the conclu- sion that these three learned gentlemen must have compared notes before they spoke. Their utterances on the Egyptian question, which, of course, is the topic they have chiefly dealt with, are almost identi- cal. Eaeh says that the Egyptian war was unneces • sary, and therefore unjust ; each complains that a Liberal Government should have brought troops from , India to Egypt, after objecting to a Conservative , Government bringing Indian troops to Malta; and with each it is a source of satisfaction that the , Island of Cyprus—the vaunted acquisition of Lord ' Beaconsfield and Lord Salisbury, and derided by the I Liberals —should have been utilized during the cam- paign. We frankly aimit that the acquisition of Cyprus has been very much derided by the Liberal I party, and by none more strongly than by some of the members of the present Cabinet; and we ! fai/now to see that the island will ever be of great value to England either in peace or war; but it should ; not be forgotten that it was not Cyprus itself so much as the mode by which it was obtained that gave rise to the violent opposition it met with in Liberal circles. The Liberal party believed that Parliament ought to have been consulted before the Anglo-Turkish; Con- vention was concluded. We all know it was signed :1 and sealed without the knowledge or consent of Par. liament. Lord Beaconsfield and Lord Salisbury entered the Berlin Conference demanding that everything ' should be fair and-above board, and that Russia, not- withstanding her great success, should not possess any advantages over the other Powers, yet the Plenipoten- tiaries of England alone violated the understanding been arrived at in this regard. When, therefore, Lord Beaconsfield was found to be playing false to the other , Powers of Europe, false to Parliament, and bringing dishonour upon the name of England, it is not sur- prising that the whole Cyprus transaction should have been derided not only by the Liberal party, but also by the country, as it certainly was at the last general election. At the same time, that is no reason why the island, having been acquired, should not have been ' utilised. la gain, with respect to the bringing of troops from India to take part in the Egyptian campaign, it was one of the very laet acte of the Government ' before the adjournment to ask the sangtion of Perna- I ment to the employment of the Indian troops, and we are happy:to think the necessary permission was cheer- fully granted. But the Conservative Government did I not consult Parliament when the Indian troops were I removed to Malta during the Russo-Turkish war. The removal of the troops on that occasion, like the Anglo- Turkish Convention,was effected in a sneaking fashion. Just before the adjournment of Parliament for the Easter recess, Sir Stafford Northcote, as the leader of the House of Commons, was asked whether he had any information to communicate to Parliament respect- ing the intentions of the Government with regard to the war, and he replied that he had not, yet scarcely had members returned to their homes than they were made acquainted, through the newspapers, of the des- patch of troops from India. In that instance the Con- servative Government wilfully deceived Parliament, whereas had it taken Parliament into its confidence all parties would most undoubtedly have loyally sup- ported it. The objection has all along been not to the employment of the Indian troops dur- ing the Russo - Turkish war, but to the flagrant violation of the Constitution in utilising them without the consent of Parliament. But it is argued that the Egyptian war was unnecessary, and therefore unjust. It is hard to tell what the Tories really want. They badgered the Government both in season and out of season to revenge the massacres at Alexandria of the iith June, to support the Khedive's authority, and to protect the Suez Canal; and now that that great water-way is safe in our keeping and our road to India is secure, that the Khedive's authority is restored and respected, and that the instigators of the massacre and of the rebel- lion as well have been brought to justice, it is urged that the war was unnecessary forsooth, and therefore unjust ! Why, it is preposterous .to talk in such a manner. All the Powers of Europe approve our action ; only the loyal and patriotic Tories of Eng- land complain ! The fact is, the work we were com- pelled to undertake in Egypt has been accomplished so swiftly, and at the same time so satisfactorily, that the Tories are disappointed and, mortified almost be- yond recovery. They hoped to make our troubles in Egypt, if sufficiently prolonged, a lever with which to again elevate them to place and power; and these legal gentlemen who are now stumping the country know very well they have "no case," though, of course, it does not prevent them following out the legal maxim under such circumstances, and soundly "abusing the other side." After all, the great fight in the coming autumn session will not be over Egypt, but over the rules of procedure, and it is a pity they are not now in force, for it is very certain that when- ever Parliament meets there will be a great deal of very unnecessary talk, and a very great deal of time wasted. We feel sure, however, that before the House again adjourns the ClOsure.will have been • agreed upon in some form or another. Mr. Gibson is dreadfally afraid lest it should be C:Osure by a bare majority ; but that we sincerely hope it may be, as it will in practice be found the best mode of dealing with obstruction. It is said there is a desire on the part of the Government to gag discussion ; yet perfect freedom of debate does not now exist, for everything is practically in the hands of the minority, whose lights, we contend, will be better guarded be a bare than by a two-thirds majority. Besides, as a bare majority decides the fate of a bill and of an Administration, in common justice such a majority Ought to be sufficient to close a debate. It is greatly to be desired that the Government on this point should remain steadfast, and we hope that nothing that may be said on the Tory benches will beguile it from its duty.

WE would direct the attention of our readers to an advertisement which appears in another page respecting the proposed Ship Canal to connect Manchester with Liverpool. The scheme is one which has receivedthe sanc- tion of a very high authority in engineering, and if the requisite means can only be raised to enable the promoters to overcome the opposition with which the project will necessarily bo met and successfully carry it through Parliament, we doubt not that the canal will become an accomplished fact. Lonsdale, Blackburn, cotton spinners and manufacturers, as T. Bolton and Co. ASSAULT BY A LA.NDLORD. —At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. Holbrook Gas- jun., James Lee, landlord or owner of the Railway Inn, Ditton, was summoned by Mary Wynne, wife of Henry Wynne, carter, of the same place, for assaulting her on Saturday last.—Mr. Husband appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Beasley for the defendant.—Mr. Husband said the complainant resided near the defendant's house, adjoining which he had a small shed. Mr. Lee had made a claim to the land upon which the shed was erected, and had taken some high-handed proceedings, having put up a barr;er to stop up the entrance; but this would probably be a question fora civil court. On the day in question Mrs. Wynne and her daughter went to the shed, when Mr. Lee suddenly pounced from his house, and a witness namee John Grace, a labourer, who was on the railway, saw him with his fist raised in the act of striking. A train at that time came up, and he did not see a blow struck. When the train had passed, he saw the woman was on the ground. She lay there for some time, and had at last to be carried into the house, where she fainted. Since then she had been attended by a doctor.—Cemplainant, John and Robert Grace, gave evidence in support of this statement.—Anuie Lewis, the married daughter of complainant, said she was with her mother at the time of her assault. Mr. Lee rushed out of his ' house, and her mother seized bold of him by the shirt front, ' and pushed him. Mr. Lee returned the push, and knocked her to the ground. She fainted.—Cross-examined by Mr. Beasley, witness denied that her mother called Mr. Lee an old villain.—Mr. Beasley, for the defence, submitted that there was no case. He contended that Mrs. Wynne was in a state of great excitement, and when Mr. Lee appeared on ' the scene she seized him by the shirt front. He put his hands on her shoulders to restrain her violence and she fell. Whilst on the ground she called him an old villain, and said she would not get up until a policeman arrived.—The Bench were of opinion the assault had been proved, and fined the defendant 10s. and lie. 61. costs, and also the cost of one witness.

A DISOBEDIENT BOATMAN —BLOCKING WID NES LOCKS —On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. Jno. Brock and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, George Foster, a boatman, was charged, that he being the owner of a certain boat, the "Tam o' Shanter," did unlawfully refuse to obey the lock- master, who had the power to direct all vessels entering in the docks.—The defendant pleaded not guilty. Mr. A. C. Preston appeared on behalf of the London and North-Wes- tern Railway Company. He quoted the section under which the summons was taken, and said the facts of the case were as follows :—On the 3rd inst. the defendant was in charge of his empty boat, which he was dragging by a rope placed round his shoulders, towards the entrance of the locks. At the same time there was a larger boat called the "Alert," laden with sand, also going towards the en- trance of the lock. It was a well-know rule of the lock that loaded vessels should have precedence of light or unloaded vessels, sa the dockmaster, who was on the qua Y wall at the time, shouted to the defendant that he must not enter the lock, but give way to the "Alert." The defendant, notwith- standing this command, still pulled his vessel towards the entrance, shouting, "I shall not. It is my turn now, and I will have it. I know the rules as well as you, and I will have my turn for you or anybody else." A woman on the boat, and who was steering, also called "He has plenty of money." The Alert was now in the entrance to the lock, and the defendant also ran his boat in the crest a "jam." When the tide receded, it being high rater, the boats rolled towards each other, so that when the tide again rose, they coukd not rise with it and the water covered them. This state of things existed until Tuesday. the 10th inst., when it was found necessary to take active measures to get the vessels loose. A gang of 15 men with pulleys and hydraulic jacks was sent to the spot' and they raised one of the flats bodily. The expense of doing this was £9 16s. But this was not the only result of this dis- obedience. Vessels were unable to enter or come out of the canal, and the company in consequence had had many claims for damage. Although it seemed a very slight matter at first, it really very seriously affected the railway company, and he asked the Bench to dal with the case ac- cordingly. He pressed the case against the defendant.—John Fox, the dockmaster, confirmed this statement, stating that there had been 50 tons of sand taken from the Alert in order to raise it. The assistant dockmaster' Charles Shore, the foreman of the engineers' department, also gave evidence.— The defendant said he was a stranger to the locks, but con- tended that he only took his turn. When the dockmaster saw him pulling in he ordered the master of the Alert also to pull in, and thus the "jam " occurred. If he (defendant) was wrong, why didn't the dock-master allow him to go in and report him, instead of allowing the " jam "to occur and "break everything."—Mr. Preston remarked that the flats had been got out without any appreciable damage.— Mr. Brock: Are there many cases of this kind ?—Mr. Fer- rand replied that there had been three since he came.—Mr. Brock said the Bonch were satisfied from the evidence be- fore them that the case was very cicar, and one of gross dis- obedience. Whenever the defendant or anybody else entered the lock, they were bound to obey the orders of the dock- master. It had always been a rule for the loadened vessels to take p-ecedence of the empty ones both in and out. The dockmaster's office was sufficiently difficult at any time, but especially was it so when his orders were disobeyed. IL was a case for a fairly heavy fine. Defendant was table to a fine of £lO, and he would -be tined £5 and costa 15s, or, in default, go to gaol for one month.

ORGAN RECITAL AT RUNCORN.—A large audience assem- bled at Halton-road Wesleyan Chapel, on Monday evening, to hear an organ recital by Miss Aslin, the organist of that place of worship. The performance was a thoroughly enjoyable one, and Miss Aslin's brilliant execution of the pieces she had chosen was received with marked expressions of approval. Her performance was of so uniform an excel- lency that it wou!d be invidious to particularise, but we may express the hope that the Runcorn public will have other opportunities of listening to Miss Aslin's performances. The programme included—
- Mari he aux Flambeaux S. Clarke. A ndante Wely. Fogue Rink. Two variations Heller. Oraw4March in D Buyton Smith. Andante Batiste Silva, Trumpets Invocation Boyton Smith

At the conclusion of the recital the Rev. George Hack said it was Miss Aslin's wish that she should not be thanked for her kindness. Judging from the way in which the audience had listened to the fine performance he was sure that was not their wish. He for one had been more than delighted, and could scarcely forbear a cheer. They were-.not only in- debted to Miss Aslin for that evening's performance but also for her services rendered to the chapel Sunday after Sunday without fee or reward. He was exceedingly glad to have this opportunity of publicly expressing his feelings and the feelings of the church to Miss Aslin for her kindness. (Ap- plause.) Mr. J. R. Frith said he heartily united in the ex- pression of thanks to 11s.s Aslin, aud he was sure he was only interpteting the feelings of those present when he said he hoped that during the winter there would be given similar recitals to the one which they had just listened to. (Applause.) It was a pity that with such a valuable in- strument, and such a player as Miss Aslin, they should be devoid of musical ti eats. He had great pleasure in second- ing the proposition moved by Mr. Hack. The motion was carried by acclamation. Mr. Hack remarked that the un- mistakable appt eciation of the audience would doubtless be an encouragement for Miss Aslin to continue in her valuable work to the chapel. A collection was made for the choir funds.

NARROW ESCAPE FROM COLLISION ON THE RAILWAY NEAR RUNCORN.—AS the 8 45 train from Chester to War- rington was approaching the junction on the London and North-Western Railway, near Halton station, on Monday morning, the 9-9 train from Runcorn was observed to be rounding the cur ve, and travelling at a good speed. The manner in which the rails cross each other at the junction, compels one train to wait until the other has passed, when two happens to be at the spot at the same time. But from the speed at which both trains were proceeding on this occasion it was evadent that this could not be done, and a collision, which could not fail to be disastrous in its consequences to both life and property, seemed unavoidable. The dangers of the situation, however, were fully grasped by the man in charge of the signals.—Ralph B azley, of Frodsharn—and he was prompt in action. With his points he turned the Warrington train on the Liverpool up line, and thus made it possible for the trains to pass each other on separate lines. It is stated that the signal was against the driver of the Runcorn train, but whether be was not aware of this, or was unable to stop his engine, cannot be stated with certainty. There is no doubt that the presence of mind displaved by Bazley averted a catastrophe ef no mean magnitude, and his conduct is deserving of more than a mere passing notice Blame, too often, is only the signal- man's portion, and there is, therefore, all the more reason why such a meritorious act as that of Bazley's should meet with a fitting reward. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT A WIDNES WORKS.—OR Thurs- day morning, a serious accident occurred to James Marsh, at the boiler corks of Mr. David Foster, Lugsdale-road, Widnes. Marsh, it seems; was helping several men to place on a bogie a boiler weigLing about 16 cwt., when the boiler slipped and rolled back. The boiler fell heavily against Marsh, knocking him down and inflicting serious injuries. Three of his ribs were broken, ad his body as very badly bruised. The outstanding liabilities of the Board at the end of the year amounted to £29,478 18s 6d, and consisted of IGans from the Public Works Commissioners. The accounts were adopted on the motion of Mr. Shaw. WELK/ CONCERT AT WIDNES.-With the object of add- ing to the fund for liquidating the debt of £460 which exists upon the Welsh Congregational Chapel, Moor-lane, Widnes, a concert of a high class character was given in the Volunteer Hall on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. Thomas, of Liverpool, presided. There was a crowded audience. The vocalists were from the choir of the Tabernacle, Liver- pool, assisted by local artistes. Mr. Thomas Owens con- ducted and presided at the harmonium. Mr. W. J. Mahon was the pianist. Mr. R. Rees (Eos Morlais), of Swansea, is a tenor singer of ability, and his rendering of "Children's home," "Good company," and" When the tide comes in," were marked by power and effect. Mrs. Lea was in fine voice, and the pieces set down to her name were sung with conspicuous taste. She was especially successful in the sang, "The lost chord." Madame Williams, who possesses a ssprano voic2 of great sweetness, sang amongst other* pieces "Within a mile of Edinbro' town," and she was encored, a compliment which was accorded all her efforts. Mr. Rees and Mrs. Williams also sang several duets with preat success. Mr. S. J. Edwards was warmly applauded for the song, " Oh, oh, the wild winds blow." The choir I sang several anthems in a manner which left little to be de- sired. The concert was a most enjoyable one.

FITRIOTJS DRIVING IT WARRINGTON.—James Cottam, a farmer's son, residing at Culcheth, was summoned at the Warrington Police Court, mu Monday, for furiously driving a horse and spring cart, and further for not keeping his cart on the right side.—On Wednesday last the defendant was driving up Church•street in a spring cart along with his mother and oth( r persons. When near the Bull's Head public-house defendant met a load of straw, which he passed on his proper side, but when near the National schools hoe-net a cab driven by William Lee. There was plenty of room for defendant to pass on his right side, but, the Chief Constable said, he was driving at such a furious rate that he ran into the cab and smashed it up entirely. The cabman waethrown over his horse, and fell on his left side on the floor. A man dragged him away, or he would have been killed; as it was, he had been under the doctor's care since. Several witnesses were called, who Yarigusly stated that defendant was driving at from five to twelve I miles an hour, and was on his wrong side lower down the street than where the accident happened. The Bench treated the two offences as one, and fined the defendant 20s. and costs.—Edward Lunt, George Drew, andßeiNiv'mee.yltturlesee, carters were charged with furious driving in on the 29th ult. On the evidence of P.C. Baxerndale and others, Luut and Drew were each fined 103 and costs. Hulse was discharged. CRICKET : WESLEY HILL 'CRICKET CLITU 7. If all I Lear is correct, and there is no reason to doubt h,ing so, sufficient ,zate-money was tilo-n to pay for 0, wt.o'e of the prizes, while the entries would, no doubt, eititt•r fuliy, or vety nearly so, pay the show yard expenses, so the additional one hundred pounds subscribed in Runcorn will be a clear benefit to the funds of the society. The great success was doubtless contributed to by the splendid weather, but there is such a large surrounding population that I think if the Cheshire Agricultural society were to visit Runcorn next year and give early intimation of their intention they would reap a large harvest, possibly gain new members, and encourage entries and exhibits from a district erroneously supposed to yield nothing except "noxious vapours."

In your report of the last meeting of the Runcorn Burial Board appears the following recommendation of its Finance Committee:—" That in future the annual instalments in re- payment of debt on the cemetery should be invested in a sinking fund, which should accumulate until it amounted to the whole of the debt." I thought it a strange recommenda- tion, ard determined to look the matter up for the benefit or information of your readers. The cemetery, lam told, has been opened for over 20 years, and its mortgage debt is still only just under six thousand pounds. If the members of the B rial Board will consult the Acts of Parliament which de- fine their powers, they may profitably be referred to section 20 of 15 and 16 Vic., c 85, which reads—" That it shall be lawful for the Board, with the sanction of the Vestry and the approval of the Commissioners of Her Majesty's Treasury, to borrow any money required for providing and laying out any burial ground. and building a chapel or chapels thereon, or any of such purposes, and to charge the future poor rates of the parish with the payment of such money and interest thereon ; provided that there shall be paid in every year, in addition to the interest of the money borrowed and unpaid, not less than one-twentieth of the principal sum borrowed, until the whole is discharged." Perhaps the report presented woull have been more complete if it had been a little more " informing " as to the above matters, and also as to the power of a Burial Board to create a sinking fund. The defeat which the Runcorn Commissioners sustained in their action against the Glycerine Works, has put them into a stafe of great perturbation. They have formed a committee to try and solve the rather peculiar question "Is the resolution entered on the minutes of the Board or te resolution published in the newspapers the correct one ? " The committee best know how they are going to proceed in their inquiry, but, whatever decision they may arrive at , it cannot have any practical effect, un- less, indeed, it emboldens them to appeal against the verdict of the magistrates who based their conclusions upon the Board's own minute. I scarcely think, however, that they will possess the hardihood to take this course after their recent unfortunate procEedings in the law caurts. But, as Dr. McDougall sententiously puts it, it is a questann affecting the honour of the Board, and cer- tainly no stain ought to be allowed to remain upon that. However, the chairman of the Board, Dr. Steele, has devised a method to ensure the correctness of all future resolutions. Each member, whea he makes a motion, has to give in a written copy, or it will not be accepted, and the unusual literary labours en- tailed upon the members at the last meeting of the Bo ird, created a little exciting confusion. Writers of resolutions were besieged with anxious advisers, who offered no doubt well meant suggestions as to how this or that motion should be drawn up; while amid the bubble of voices, the chairman could te heard calling for order, with worry depicted upon his countenance. Such was the scene described to me, but in a short time the new method, I fear not, will be fully mastered by our local legislators, as they seem to be exhibi- ting an almost feverish anxiety to keep within the limits of the law. I trust, however, they will not become martyrs to their love for order, which permeates them from the chair- man downwards.

The members of the Irish Parliamentary part y—or rather I those who are led by Mr. Parnell—meet in Dublin next week, and in view of the peremptory closing of the Irish Land League fund in America the meeting should be more than usually interesting. The close of the fund was an- nounced in last week's Irish World, and the reason is said to be "because there is no longer a Land League in exis- tence." This, of course, is quite true, for the organisttion was suppressed by the Government some time ago, but the wonder is, if that be the real reason why the American fund is closed, that it was not wound up months ago. The con- tributions have been liberal, it will be generally admitted, amounting to no less than 345,548 dols., and it is surprising that the money should have poured in so plentifully seeing that no account was ever rendered of the expenditure. And where has all the money gone to? for Mr. Egan, the trea- surer, is stumped up, and he has been compelled ta announce that in consequence of the stoppage of supplies the Irish members of Parliament who have hitherto been paid for their services and patriotism can no longer receive remuneration. The Irish World is despondent over the precent state of Ir4land, and maintains that Ireland would have been better off to-day had not the people been diverted by Parliamentary agitation; and the founder of the Land League, Mr. Michael Davitt, in what has been designated a "funeral speech," at Wexford, on Sunday, dolefully deplored the col- lapse of the crusade against landlordism. For my part, I fail to see any necessity for this repining ; for if it was the object of the League to overthrow landlordism and to secure the land for the people, that has been practically accom- plished. It is paten', to every one tbat the Land and the Arrears Acts are working a reformation in Ireland far beyond anything which could have been expected when the League was founded, and even if the League existed now in all its pristine vigour, I question if it would be of much utility, except in finding money for idlers to spend indis- creetly.

The Reform Club having become more social than politi- cal, a movement is now on foot to establish a "National Liberal Club" in the metropolis, and I commend the scheme to the notice of the readers of The Examiner. The move- ment originated at a meeting of the Century Club held in May, and the amount of support which it has already received augurs well for its future success. It is proposed that the premises shall, when erected, be central, spacious, convenient, and inexpensive; so as to be a place of meeting for Liberals coming up to London from the provinces, and a medium of interchange of views between London and the rest of the kingdom. It is intended that the club shall have all the app)intments of a first-rate London club. The reading-room will be supplied with all the principal provincial, as well as the London papers and periodicals; and in addition to the usual writing, billiard, and smoking rooms, there shall be private rooms for the business appointments of members at a moderate charge. There shall also be a commodious room for meetings and conferences ; and the upper part of the club shall, if pos- sible, be so arranged as to afford bedroom accommodation for country members. This latter is a very desirable feature ; but in addition thereto, it is hoped that if such a club were established the many associations in London and the provinces which deal with Liberal organisation and reform would consider it desirable to have their London offices in the same building as the club, and for this arrange- ments will be made. The subscriptions are to be reasonable. For members not resiuent within 10 miles of the club no entrance fee will be payable, and their annual subscription will be only £2; but the entrance fee for members resident within that limit will be £6, and the subscription £4. Mem- bers, however, of any bona fide social club, the annual sub- scription to which is not less than £5, will be exempt from entrance fee. The scheme has already received the adhe- sion and support of Lord Granville, Lord Northbrook, Lord Kensington, Lord Rosebery, Lord R. Grosvenor, and a gt eat many members of Parliament ; whilst the officers of 61 Liberal associations have approved of the club, and in most cases have expressed a desire to join it. The club will un- doubtedly meet a long felt want, and 1 heartily wish it every success. FLACCUS.

ATTEMPTED RESCUE. Thomas Kincherley WEB brought up in custody at the Widnes Police Court, on Mon- day, charged with resisting P.C. George Dunsdale, on the Bth inst., whilst in the execution of his duty. It appeared that P.C.'s Dunsiale and _Brown apprehended a man, who the prisoner attempted to rescue, but did not succeed. It was elicited that the prisoner was drunk, and Mr. Inspector B itnett said under the circumstances, he would withdraw the present charge, for which he would substitute that of drunkenness. To this charge the prisoner pleaded guilty, and he was fined 53. and costa.

APPEAL TO THE YOUNG LADIES OF THE DAY AND BOARDING SCHOOLS OF LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE. Sir,—A very happy thought was suggested a few months ago to the young ladies of the boarding and day schools ef this district, that they should, by their united contributions, establish a home for their poorer sisters, who, in the provi- dence of God, are left orphans, homeless, and destitute in our great city. Since the idea was thrown out, the Bishop of Manchester and Mrs. Fraser have been much interested in it, and the latter has become the treasurer of a fund for this purpose, called "The School Girls' Home" Fund. The young ladies in many of the schools have taken the matter up warmly, with the full sanction of the principals, and s. have sent Mrs. Fraser a total from 83 schools of £415 ks 25. 2d. We find the cost of a house for the purpose to be £6OO, consequently the balance still required is £lB4 17s. 10d. Seeing that so largo a portion of the sane required is raised, and as many destitute little ones were waiting admission, our committee have actually taken the house, in _ hope that when the effort becomes better known, the full amount will be raised. The sum still required could easily bkobtained in other ways, but Mrs. Fraser and the commit- ! tee are most anxious that this good work should be done entirely by the school girls, so that we can put the following intimation in the lobby :—" The School Girls' Home; the gift of the school girls of Lancashire and Cheshire to their poorer sisters." We are sure that our young friends everywhere will be glad to know that their effort is about to be accomplished, and it is with confidence we appeal to ' those who have not yet contributed to share in the good work. We are requested by Mrs Fraser to say that she will gladly receive and acknowledge the smallest sum sent from any school, or by any individual yonng lady for this object, addressed to her, Bishop's Court, Higher Broughton. We may say that the Home will be opened by the Bishop and Mrs. Fraser, on Saturday, November llth.—We are, yours, etc., LEONARD K. SHAW, GILBERT R. KIRLEW, • Hen. Secs. to the Boys' and Girls' Refuges • and Homes, Strangeways. October ith, 182. WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. Sir,—l have been examining the balance sheet and read- ing the report of this society, and regret to say that both are unsatisfactory, and indicate that the society is not in a healthy condition. As a subscriber, and one wishing to see the society something more than a society for giving two concerts in the season as payment for the subscription, I , venture to suggest to the committee the desirability of study- ing the rules, and as far as possible adhering to them. The ' object of the society is the cultivation of vocal and instru- mental music, but of late years no attempt has been made to I cultivate the latter, but I see in the balance sheet a very large sum is spent in professional players. In my opinion, if this money was spent in training a band, the society and the town would be the better for it, and the subscribers much better satisfied than they are at present. But so long as the management sneer and carp at any performances which fall short of a very high standard for amateurs, I fear there will be a difficulty created by themselves, and serve as an excuse for doing nothing. I wish to call the attention of the members to this, because a good voice is not given to many, but given the opportunity there are many musicians in Warrington who desire to join the society as instrumentalists. Until the committee make the society a popular one, by admitting all to the advantages of a musical training, both vocal and instrumental, and undertaking elementary instruction also, it will fail to command the support and the sympathy required. On all sides we hear complaints of the want of energy and insight into the real wants of the town. The society occupies the ground, and there is no chance for two societies, neither is it desirable ; but this points to the necessity of more energetic action on the part of the present committee to deal with the whole question of musical training. Many subscribers are waiting patiently in the hope that the committee will see its way to clear off the debt, and to put matters in such a form that the society shall command the necessary support by its usefulness.—Yours truly, A SUBSCRIBER.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT. BATURDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Burgess. The only case of Wet est is reported in another column. MoNDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Major Cartwright, and Councillor Fatrclough. A DRAB COB OF COAL.—Mary Dodd, married woman, 1, Quay Fold, was charged with having at mie night, on Saturday. stolen a lump of coal, value 3d, the property of Wm. Butterton. Liverpool-road.—Prosecutor's son was in the kitchen when he saw the prisoner in the yard, He followed her out into Quay Fold, and she fell across her door-step, dropping a piece of coal In the fall.—Prisoner denied the charge, and said she was in bed at the time 4 the alleged robbery, but a witness stated he was sure the prisoner was the woman who fell with the coal.— She was sent to prison for a month with bard labour. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH—John Lyon was fined 2s 6d, including costs, for wheeling a coal waggon on the footpath in Pierpoint- street. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES —The following persons were each fined ss, including mats, for not sending their children to school :—Thomas Crank, forgeman, Lythgoe's-lane; Thomas 1 Flanagan, labou-er, Silver-square; Thomas Lawless, labourer, Silver-street; Thomas Briars. labourer, Winwick-street; Cor- nelius Lennon, forgeman, Portland-street; Thamas Cunliff e, forgeman, Back Angel Ya: d ; James Sharp, glass-maker, Greenall-street; William McCarty, glass-maker, Tilley-street ; John Hardy, tanner, Did Court, and James Evans, butcher. New-road, I atchford A YOUNG INCORRIGIBLn.—Annie Marra. a young woman, was committed for a month's hard labour for being drunk and disorderly. The prisoner had been several times previously convicted, and was only discharged on Saturday for a similar offence in consideration of her being summoned to appear before the Bench to-day.—The Bench, in committing her to prison. said she was quite incorrigible. PEACE BREAKERS.—George Phillips, William Richardson, Richard Banner, Robert Hayes, Alfred Groves, and David Smith, were each bound over for breaches of the peace. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks. LNTOXICANTS.—Richard Filburn, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street on the previous day, was fined 7s. 6d., including costs and Michael Brett, an ex-soldier, was charged with a like offence in Nendrick-street, but was dis- missed on promising to leave the town. THURSDAY —Before Captain Litton. The cases of interest will be found reported in another column. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Alderman Chandley. UNION CASE.—Geo,ge Howaad, painter. Latchford, was sum- moned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute to the maintenance of his mother. Mary Howard, who is chargeable to the common fund of the War- rington Union—Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Guardians, supported the summons, and Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendant.—lt was shown that Mrs. Howard kept lodgers and went out charring, but as she had several children to main- ' tain she was compelled to seek relief.—Mr. Davies contended that as the woman was not an impotent woman the defendant was not liable.—The Clerk held that Mrs. Howard was able to maintain herself, and said a brother was not bound to provide for his brothers and sisters, as he was for his fatherand mother. —The Bench said they could not make an order. ASSAULTS —Michael McLoughlin was summoned for assault- ing Peter Carey on the 3rd inst., and Mary McLoughlin (wife) and Mary McLoughlin (daughter) were summoned for assault- ing Mary Carey, wife of Peter.—Peter Cary had a large portion of his head covered with plaister, his wife had hex left arm in bandages, the male defendant's head was starred with plaister, and his wife's eyes were much discoloured, the whole of the injuries having apparently been caused by a hammer, hat:het, and "pot stick," which were produced in court —The defend- ants were bound over to keep the peace for six months; and the Bench thought the complainants as bad as defendants, and said if they had been summoned they would have bound them over as well.—Joseph Ellis, Turner-street, was bound over to keep the peace for assaulting John James Ihomas Drinkwater. 7 PROVOKING LANGUAGE.—Sarah Dagnall, summoned for using language towards Ellen Gleave calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, was bound over to keep the peace; and James Green was also bound over to keep the peace for using similar language toward.s his mother, Sarah Green. and his sister, Sarah Jane Smith.

" DESTRUCTIVE " SPORT. r Sir,—Permit me to attempt to answer seriously " New- tonian's" communication of September 30th. He says : " The feeling among the better-to-do people here was cer- tainly a very mixed emotion, when they heard of the pro- posal to hive a coursing ground in the neighbourhood, and they felt as if they had just found an exponent of these feel- ings in 'Anglo-Scotus.' " Considering that four months have now elapsed since the appearance of my first letter on the subject, it does not say much for the depth or sincerity of the emotion felt by the better-to-do people alluded to, that they have remained silent all this time. Were I inclined to sneer or turn peevish, I might ask "Newtonian" whether the "mixed emotion" has anything to do with the " mixy maxy "way in which he has all along approached the sub- ject. If " Newtonian " will take the trouble to re-read my letters of June 10th and September 2nd, he will „see that I have used no hesitating,' or halting language in denouncing the cruelty of the practice of breeding hares for the sole purpose of publicly coursing them. But I have been care- ful to distinguish "cruelty "from "legitimate sport," i.e., the destruction of all kinds of game or other animals that take tithe of the farmer or owner or cultivator of the soil, when their numbers reach such a point as to interfere with what is termed "nature's balance," or " the survival of the fittest." Again, "Newtonian "remarks :—" In a few weeks we shall bee° the first coursing meethig, and may see vast crowds of people to witness this cruel sport. And not less cruel because, as 'Anglo-Scotus' says, the ffish of the hare is better food for man—["better for the table" are my words]—when chased than when shot. Probably one of the last thoughts to enter the minds of the coursing com- mittee will be as to whether the dead bares are fit for food or not, although they may be quite as humane as many of the thousands who will go to witness the coursing." Before I make any comment upon this lame attempt to twist or contort my plain and as I consider straightforward admission of the right of gentlemen and others to course or hunt the hare on their own estates or farms, contained in my letter of September 2nd, allow me to draw the attention of " New- tonian " and his friends of the 'mixed emotion" to the following criticism, taken from the World of Saturday last, • a so-called "society" paper, let them bear in mind : " Sportsmen of the old school would have been horrified at the idea of coursing in September, opposed as such a farce is to all the instincts of a sportsman. It has, however, be- come the fashion of late years thus to commence out of season, but fortunately the sport, so called, has never before been associated with such scenes of butckery as those which occurred at the meets held last week at Kempton. Under the old system of finding the game before coursing it, the hares had some chance of escaping; but here they had none, for of the 38 courses first decided 36 hares were done to death. Such proceedings call for earnest protest from all -- ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT. who have any feeling for dumb animals. DISORDERLY CtraRecTERY:-:-.TOseph Taylor was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Halton on the 4th instant, an on the evidence of P.S. Grounds he was fined 103 and costs.— Catheline McVann was charges with using obscene language in Mersey-street on the 25th inst.—P.S. McMichael proved the ease, and the defendant was fined 5s and c,sts 9s 6d, or, in de- fault. 14 days' hard labour.—For being drunk and disorderly in Church-street, on Saturday night, John Rafferty was fined 10s and costs 8s 4d.—P.o. Finney and Inspector Hollingworth gave evidence. —On the evidence of P.O. Wallace, Catherine Head, a stranger, was fined 5s and costs 6s 4d for being drunk and disorderly in Meney-street on Saturday evening.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. H, dossage. thscEmAiltous.—George Burke, John Mannion, Michael Campbell, Michael Eavers, and Stephen Kelly were each charged with drunkenness, and fined in sums varying from 5s and costs to 103.—Mary Clarke was charged with committing a breach of the peace on the 22nd July, and at her own request she was committed to gaol for 14 days. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. B. Hall. BREACHES CF THE PEACE.—ElizAbeth Cross and Alice Wil- liamson were bound over to keep the peace for three months for creating a disturbance.
