Reformed Church. (Applause.) , . The Rev. T. RippoN said he was present as a humble member of another church simply to wish his friend, Mr. Mules, and his co - workers the heartiest "God-speed." He supposed there were very many about 'there who knew that he was a Wesleyan Methodist, and he sometimes heard Wesleyan Methodists saying of themselves they were the friends of all and the enemies of none. He was present that afternoon to give expression to that senti- ment. John Wesley, in one of his standard sermons used these words, "Let your oponent have all the bigotry to himself." (Laughter.) He believed all who knew his face knew that he had not got a drop of bigot's blood in his veins, for he hated bigotry as he hated strong drink. The late Charles Kingsley, he believed, in his "Alton Locke" gave expression to his (the speaker's) views when he said a new church or new school he always rejoiced over. Charles Kingsley expressed himself in that book in this fashion: "And yet it was a pleasant sight as every new church is to the healthy-minded man, let his religious opinions be what they may. A fresh centre of ; civilisation, mercy, comfort for weary hearts, relief from ; frost and hunger; a fresh centre of instruction, humanising, I disciplining, however meagre in my eyes, to hundreds of little savage spirits; altogether a pleasant sight." To him it was a very pleasant sight to see that building going up, but he fancied that to some people it was not a very pleasant sight. He fancied that the devil, if he might use the name in that very respectable audience, would not regard that as a very pleasant sight. He did not suppose some of his enemies, the publicans, would regard that as a pleasant sight. He fancied there were some members, and perhaps ministers of other churches, for other reasons, who did not regard that as a very pleasant sight, and perhaps would look upon Mr. Mules as an opponent. As a Christian minister he would like publicly to declare that lie did not regard Mr. Mules as an opponent, indeed he was inclined to think Mr. Mules would help him as he hoped to help Mr. Mules—that Mr. Mules would improve his congregations as he hoped to improve his. He prayed that Mr. Mules would preach so, and work so, and prove a faithful minister of the Lord Jesus Christ, that his church would be such an active church, such a soul saving church that all other churches in Warrington would be anxious to enter into the lists with him in a holy rivalry. He regarded the church as the church of Christ, thus as Dr. Arnold, of Rugby, said "the true conception of the work of the church of Christ upon earth is this: to make our world more like heaven and men more like God." (Hear, hear.) He had only to say, in closing, in the words of an Indian savage addressed to his own tribe, but which might be equally addressed to them," May your council fire never be ex- tinguished,and your sky ever be without a Coed." ( Applause.) The ceremony of laying the stones was then, r oceeded

with. Mr. HALL, addressing Mr. Alderman Davies,said the vestry of Emmanuel Church, on behalf of themselves and the members of the congregation, had deputed him to present him with that trowel to lay one of the memorial stones o f Emmanuel Church, the first Reformed Church in Lanca- shire. He did so with great pleasure, bee,au3e he knew he (Alderman Davies) was conversant with the reasons that had obliged them to leave the Established Church. It was to him a matter of deep regret that a Reformed Church of England should be needed; but events in the Establishment clearly showed that the battle of the Reformation would have to be fought over again. "A house-divided against itself cannot stand ; " but they trusted that House of God, whose memorial stones they were met that day to lay, would ever be a watch tower against the enemy, whether from without or within ; and that its members would be true to reformation principles, being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets Jesus Christ himself being the chief , corner stone. (Applause.) Alderman DAVIES then adjusted the stone, and presently declared it to be well and truly laid. The stone bore the following words: "This stone was laid by Joseph Davies, J.P., Monday, October 9th, 1882." In addressing the assembly, the Alderman said it was a great pleasure to him to be present, for he believed it was the bounden duty of all Christians, whatever particular denomination they might be connected with, when they were called upon to assist all other workers in Christ to develop the particular department which they thought was best for the glorification of their great national Church—which was the worship of their Lord Jesus Christ. All he could say was that that church and all other churches for the promotion of Christianity, whatever denomination it might be, would re- ceive from him all the support he could give. He expressed how pleased he was that the inhabitants of Warrington had shown their interest in the proceedings that day by assembling in each vast numbers, and said it must be gratifying to the promoters of Emmanuel Church to know that they had the sympathy of the townspeople." (Ap- plause. Mr. E. JEWICES, on behalf of the vestry and building committee of the Reformed Church, then presented Mr. Armitage with a trowel. He said that in asking Mr. Armi- tage to perform that little act of kindness on their behalf they believed that he was ever ready and ever willing to help them to maintain and uphold the Biblical Protestant, evangelical principles of the Church of their forefathers; and their prayer was that he might long be spared to per- form similar acts of kindness. (Applause.) Mr. ARMITAGE then took the trowel, spread the mortar, and the stone being lowered into position, declared it truly laid. Having done so, he remarked that when he was in- vited by their vestry to discharge that duty, if he had any hesitation in responding to their appeal it did not arise from any want of sympathy with their movement. The Re- formed Church was a church in which the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ would be preached; and although there miaht be minor differencss of church government and discipline between him and the church with which he worshipped and other churches, still if the gospel was preached, if evangelical truth was taught, if the Lord Jesus Christ was honoured and glorified and worshipped by the community assembled for the purpose of worship, he esteemed it an honour and privilege to be associated with them in their work. (Hear, hear.) The number of people who were assembled there that day gave an indication of the interest that was felt in the movement. He could say with those who had spoken before him, from his heart, "God speed you in your work," and might that building last many years, until it became too small for their members, until they might have to enlarge it or build another church in its place. (Applause.) A collection was then taken, and Mr. Hall laid upon the stone a cheque for £5 from Mr. Peter Smith, a cheque for a like amount from Mr. John Nunnerley, a small sum of money (£1 7s 61) collected from various sources; Alder- man Davies deposited £lO on the stone, and Mr. Armitage ' £5; and the total collodion amounted to 439_105.

The Rev. TCDOR ROGERS afterwards gave an address, in I which he stated that the constitution and Prayer-book of 1 the Church were so formed that they could not possibly be I altered except the whole feeling of the Church changed. I They could not fix them for future generations; it would I not be right for them to de so. All they conld say was that for this generation they should be as they were, ' and if they wanted the Church to be carried on in the next generation as it was in this they I should teach it their children. They should look after the children who would be the future congregation, I and they would cook after their children in the succeeding I generation, and if they would only do that they need never ' fear that the building would be used for any purpose but that ' for which it was really intended. (Applause.) The Doxology was sung, and the proceedings terminated. After the ceremony a tea meeting, at which about 500 persons were present, was held in the Public Hall. On the removal of the tables the Alpine Choir gave their usaal entertainment on behalf of the building fund of the church. The programme gave the utmost satisfaction to the audience, Iwhich filled every part of the hall, and the concert resulted lin the building fund being augmented by the sum of £23. During the interval tk,e Rev. W. MuLEs proposed, and Mr. J. HALL ..,econded a rote ,of thanks to Professor Andre, who briefly replied.

After referring to the size of several towns in the diocese, his Lord- ship said it was baffling to the imagination to suppose what Liverpool would be by and by. He assured them when he came as bishop of Liverpool to take stock of the whole state of the diocese, to examine the number of parishes, to con- sider the population, and look at the number of clefg,', /218 heart really sank within him. People were very fond of saying Liverpool was a very rich diocese, and that they needed no help, but people did not remember that in many respects the diocese was worse off than any diocese in Eng- land. They had no cathedral, no dean, no chapter, only six rural deans, and six deacons. As to rich parishes, they had certainly a number they could count upon their fingers, but when they took away Winwick and another or two there were very few good livings left. The majority of them were very pour indeed; and they had better call them starvings. That was the state of things they had to face' and one point they had before them was what could they do to aid more than they had done this society. Leaving the New Artesian Well, at Parkside, not teithom a passing thought concerning the Abyssinian Well or bore- hole at the glass works, or gas works, the very mention of which is becoming a" bore," we make our way by the path leading from the former station, which we observe is fenced off and made into a dwelling-house, and the world rushes past it as if it had never baen one of the most important stations on the line half a century ago. The earth thrown out at that time is seen a few score yards from the station, and rentinds one of those earthworks of which we have been reading so much lately, ana the il:usion is kept up by the sound of rifle shooting on the range behind it. Colliers, however, with all the drawbacks of their condition and calling when at work always live in a very equable temperature, and so far have much less to complain of than people who work above ground; and,indeed, this fact accounts in some measure for the liking which they generally conceive for their calling and vocation' and accounts also for the reluctance with which they leave it, and when they do leave it, for the readiness with which they return to it. But trail° has been bad enough there of late, so we will content ourselves with wishing and hoping for possible things—and one is a return of prosperity with good trade, which with two political clubs they surely ought to contrive between them to get for the good people of Golborne, from which no one returns dissatisfied when once he gets to know them. After making a call, ' which led us to the above renerks, we make our way to Ash- ton, or, as some of the women there unconsciously pronounce it with a fine a, as if it were " 2Eschen," past some brick- making works, where, however, trade seems to have been good, for there are many new and substantial houses lately erected. Nearing Dovecot Farm, we find our former view of the woodland hidden away behind a wood fence some 10 or 12 feet high, which begins at the Keeper's Lodge in the lane higher up, and goes to Ashton Heath, where it joins a wall which forms the boundary there, and on the other side of the town re-commences at Haydock Lodge gate, and is continued to Penny-lane end, where there is an ellipse which will afford room for ticket collectors' boxes, and room for a very large crowd to move about without obstructing the highway, and the gate-house already there may in time become a resi- dence for seine person in charge at that point. At the en- trance near Mr. Mercer's house is another similar ellipse of 20 or 30 yards in depth by some 50 or 60 in length. Avenues lead up from each entrance, and the whole ex- panse of 420 acres will form one of the finest coursing grounds imaginable ; and the Asylum to the north-west end of it is not an inelegant structure, having been at one time the residence of the Lords of the Manor, and later the scene of some of the exploits of that verdant green gentle- man, Valentine Voi, whose veracious history was among the first printed at Newton. Some other celebrity in the village at the Heath end has recorded his opinion of all this in the terse and phonetic phrase expressive of his dis- gust at all this fencing by writing in a good firm hand " Hyde Park," " Hyde Park," in fifty places at least, for the park is perfectly hidden and impervious to all who will not pay to see its beauties and participate in its pleasures. The work seems to have been thoroughly well done while they were at it, and time has not as yet made any chink in the woodwork whereat prying eyes may feast their gaze, being open only to him who pays. Crossing the Heath to do our visiting we come upon a merry-go-round wrought by steam, where juveniles are mounted and dismounted thick and fast amid a crowd of curious onlookers, and hastening on we hear six o'clock chiming, and peep in at St. Thomas's Church, which attendants are preparing for the morrow. Here we are favoured with an opinion on the farce we recently went through in our election of Commis- sioners, when the popular candidates were left in the lurch, for they manage things better in Ashton they believe, bet of course that is a matter of opinion.

REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT FRODSHAM : SERMON AND LECTIDRE.—A. sermon was preached by the Rev. Peter Mackenzie, of Bradford, in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Friday afternoon, when a good congregation was present. The text was taken from the 9th chapter of St. Matthew, Ist and 2nd verses, ani the discourse was given in the rev. gentleman's happiest manner. It would be impossible not to follow a sermon preached by the Rev. Peter Mackenzie, as such an interesting vein pervades the whole sermon that its lessons are at once understood. The lecture in the even- ing was on "General Joshua and his mighty conquests," when Mr. Thomas Norman, of Runcorn, took the chair, and there was a large attendance. The meeting was opened by singing a hymn, after which the Rev. J, M. Bamford engaged in prayer. The Chairman said he considered it an honour ard pleasure to preside at the meeting; and previous to introducing the lecturer he dwelt upon the astonishing results which had been accomplished by Methodism in a little over 100 years on the principle of voluntaryism. and reminded them that with their splendid chapel, organ, and prince of preachers in their minister, the Rev. J. M. Bam- ford, they might by the same system have the chapel crowded. Mr. Mackenzie, in the course of his lecture, traced the mighty conquests of General Joshua, and roused the patriotic feelings of his audience by his reference to the military successes of the General. The lecture was much enjoyed throughout, and the usual votes of thanks to the chairman and Mr. Mackenzie brought the meeting to a close.
IIUTTON.

ROBBING A FELLOW LODGER. Charles Porter was I charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with stealing an overcoat, pair of trousers, and a shirt from Jas. Cowen's, at Huyton Quarry, on November 30th last.—The prisoner lodged at the house with a young man named Robt. Bannister. They slept together, and at six o'clock on the morning of the 30th November Bannister went to work, leaving prisoner in bed, and the clothes which belonged to him near the foot of the bed. On returning from work in the evening, the prosecutor found the prisoner had gone away and taken the articles named in the charge. He had not seen him since until that morning.—Prisoner was com- mitted for trial THE PRESCOT GUARDIANS AND THE HUTTON OTHRSBERE. —On Tuesday, at Prescot Petty Sessions, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and J. C. Gamble, Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Guardians, preferred a complaint against Messrs. Hughes and Bushby, overseers of Huyton-with-Roby, for non-payment of two contribution orders, made respectively on the 6th of April and 27th July. The order on the 6th April was for the sum of £1,926, and that of the 27th July for £447. Since receiving the order of the Guardians to take proceedings, the overseers had paid into the treasurer's hands the sum of £447 due upon the order dated 27th July; and the complaint was therefore now for non-payment of the balance, £1,026. After quoting the law upon the sub- ject, Mr. Hartley was proceeding to put in several docu- ments, when Mr. Hughes (barrister), who appeared for the overseers, admitted that the Union was properly consticuted, that Huyton-with-Roby was one of the townships, that the call had been properly made, and that it had not been paid. —Mr. Thomas Parkinson was then called, and he stated that he served a duplicate of the order for £1,926 upon Mr. Hughes.—Mr. C. W. Comer, treasurer to the Union, said the overseers of Huyton had paid nothing since the 25th Sep- tember. The previous payment was made on the 30th December, 1881. He had not received anything on account of the contribution order dated 6:13, April.—The Clerk then produced a letter from Mr. Hughes stating, in reply to a letter to the overseers threatening proceedings if the de- mands of the Guardians were not met, that he would be glad to hear the Guardians had carried out their intention' --Mr. Hartley then gave evidence. He admitted that the £447 was to meet the demands of the county upon the Union, and that it had been usual to state that it was for county purposes on the order, but it was not done in the . last instance in consequence of what the new auditor had said.—Mr. Hughes proceeded to question witness as to how the contribution orders were made out, and to show that other townships besides Huyton were in arrear.—Mr. Hughes, in addressing the Bench on behalf of the overseers, pointed out that the arrears had been allowed to .run on for years, that it was obvious larger calls were re- quired from non-defaulting townships than would otherwise , be required, and that this was an injustice to these townships. The overseers had no personal interest in the matter, but they felt that the course of proceeding adopted by the Union was not a proper one, that something ought to be done to resist it, and they thought this was the right mode , of ventilating the subject and bringing about a more jest and equitable state of things. They never heard of any such

DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Sessions-room, on Thursday, Mr. E. Greenell in the chair. There were also present :—Messrs. Joseph Cooper John Mayer, James Knowles, Peter Percival, Wm. Bradford, Jas. Parr, Thomas Bennett, Abram Kenworthy, J. S. Rigby, P. Darbyshire, H. Houghton, W. M. Salt, T. S. Burgess, J. Weir, James Handley, J. Barker, H. Linaker (clerk), and J. Darbyshire (surveyor). MAIN ROADS ACCOUNT.—The CLERK said he had received tbe. sum of £147 6s. 51. from the county treasurer, for part payment of main roads, and it had been passed to the treasurer of that Board. FINANCE COMArtrrEE.—Accounts amounting to £lBB. 16s. were examined and recommended to be paid by cheque, and accounts amounting to £l3 15s. 3i were ordered to be paid by the surveyor from his petty cash account. £372 Os. 8.1. had been expended by the surveyor on the roads for manual and team labour during the past quarter. A cheque for £4OO sias signed for the surveyor's expenses' for manual and team labour daring the current quarter. The balance in the treasurer's hands, up to the present time, was £1,595 16s. 4d. THE SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—The SURVEYOR reported that the highway at Red-lane Bridge was frequently being damaged by the Warrington Waterworks-Co. whilst flushing main pipes, and it was desirous to pave about 12 square yards with sets round the flushing valve. He had spoken frequently on the subject to Mr. Ross, who had told him that the Waterworks Co. did not balieve in repairing the highways.—On the suggestion of the CHAIRMA,N, Mr. WEIR moved, Mr. KNowLEs, seconded, and it was agreed, that the Surveyor report the matter to the Clerk, so that he could write to Mr. Ross.—Mr. BENNETT called attention to the impassable state of road leading from Daresbury to Keck- wick through the bows of the trees growing oat on each side of the road.—The CHAIRMAN thought that the Surveyor should see Sir Gilbert GreenalPs and Sir Richard Brooke's agents as to lopping the trees on that road.—The CLERK suggested that the Board should have some notices printed, and sent round to the various land proprietors asking them to keep the trees lopped.—On the proposition of Mr. PER- CIVAL, seconded by Mr. BENNETT, the circulars were ordered to be printed. ROAD ALTERATION AT WALTON SUPERIOR.—Mr. T. S. BURGESS, waywarden for Walton Superior, submitted a plan for the improvement of the road near Brook House, Stockton Heath. He stated that if the Board would give a strip of land, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., had consented to give a piece of land to effect the improvement, as the road was very narrow. He also proposed to drain one side of the road.— On the motion of Mr. WEIR, seconded by Mr. PERCIVAL, the sanction of the Board was given for the alterations to be _ _ _

_ made subject to the approval of the surveyor. ALTERATION TO THE BROOK BRIDGE IN HATTO7.4r—LANE. —Attention was called to the dangerous state of the Brook bridge, in Hatton-lane. As a portion of the bridge was broken down, the Board directed the Surveyor to get a battle- ment built for same, at a cost of about .£2 10 —This was -all the business of importance.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION AT
div.p: THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION AT
BRISTOL.

On Monday night the 43rd Autumnal Session of the Con- gregational Union of England and Wales was inaugurated at Bristol by a devotional service in Brunswick Chapel. Up to that time 1,030 ministers and delegates had notified their presence to the secretary, and with these as well as with the general public the building was crowded to the doors. After prayer by the Rev. Samuel Hebditch, the Rev. Eustace R. Conder,-D.D., of Leeds, delivered an address on spiritual culture. The minister, he said, should possess consecration to his work, and adAptability to his surroundings, if he would be spiritually cultured. The secrets of success which were the tests of culture would be found in spirituality, prayerful- ness, and high-toned piety, but with all this there should be likewise sympathy. The service was concluded with prayer by the Revs. Frederick Hall and Mr. Blackie. The business of the Union commenced on Tuesday under the presidency of the Rev. Dr. Macfadyen, of Manchester. The President based his openiug address on the words " Faithful in a very little, faithful also in Much." Reply- ing to the objection of many persons that church questions were matters of indifference, " as trivial as the politics of a rookery," he instanced the teachings of the late Dr. Pusey, and said that whether his followers had been called Puseyites, Tractarians, or Ritualists, their labours and suc- cesses proved that the man was ignorant of human nature who treated such Matters as little and unimportant. He conceded, however, that questions of church order were little compared with the weightier matters of Christianity, and of these matters he treated in a long and eloquent dis- course. A resolution was passed in favour of promoting simultaneous local examinations as a means of extending a knowledge of the Scriptures among the young, and also one in furtherance of the work of the Special Commission on middle-class education. In moving this latter resolution, Mr. J. C. Williams complained of the Premier's disregard of their request for the appointment of a Nonconformist on ithe Charity Commission. At Wednesday's meeting of the Union a petition in favour of stopping the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sundays was unanimously adopted and signed by the president, Dr. Mac- fadyen. A statement of the position of the Jubilee Fund was submitted by the Rev. Dr. Hannay, from which it ap- peared that the total amount received up to the 30th of Sep- tember was £lBO,OOO. Appropriations had been made, in- cluding £50,000 for the liquidation of chapel debts, leaving a balance of £62,102. During the year the receipts on account of this fund had been £43,427. Addresses of con- congratulation were presented by delegates from various Free Cuurches, includinv the Baptists, Wesleyans, and Presbyterians. In the course of a discussion on evangelical agency the operations of the Salvation Army were con- sidered. Daring the day three sectional meetings were held. In the evening there was a large temperance meet- ing in the Colston Hall, under the presidency of Sir E. Baines. The meeting of the Union was continued at Btistol on 'Thursday, when a resolution was passed urgently entreat- ing the 'Government, in accordance with the express pro- visions of the Boer Convention, to take steps to effectually prevent the threatened ruin of peace, civilisation, and 'Christianity in Bechuana by incursions of certain Boers from the Transvaal. A letter was read from Earl Granville, in reply to the question whether any official authority had been given at home for the action of our troops at Cairo at I the ceremony of the procession of the Sacred Carpet. His Lordship said he had no information as to the part which ; the British troops took in the procession. In India he I believed that it was the custom for troops to attend at such I ceremonies at courts of `native princes. They pay honour not to the religious ceremony, but to the parson of the chief of state, as was probably the case at •Cairo. A deputation of clergymen of the Established Church, headed by the Very ! Rev. the Dean of Bristol, Dr. Elliott, waited on the assembly.

div.head: BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL ON HIS
div.p: THE BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL ON HIS
DIOCESE. MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

The Bishop of Liverpool presided, on Thursday afternoon, at a meeting of the Society for Promoting the Employment of Additional Curates, held in the Council Camber, at the Town Hall. There were also present the Revs. S. Wilkin- son, M. Schsnberg, W. H. Williams, J. Ward, F. W. Cory, W. W. Pomeroy, J. Brame (secretary), and E. C. E. Carle- ton (local hon. sec.), Messrs. John Hatton) Tauranac, A. Reid, &c. Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from the Rural Dean (Rev. Canon Hopwood), Messrs. W. Sharp, R. Davies,:J. R. Buckton, and Wm. Owen. —The Rev. J. BRAME observed that the position of the Addi- tional Curates Society in the diocese of Liverpool just now was a very critical one, as the position of every society must be that had for its object the increase of the ministry of the Church in the face of the enormous increase of popu- lation that they had in this diocese. He believed with the exception of the dioceses of London and Liverpool, there was no diocese in which the increase of population was so great as it was in the diocese of Liverpool. It was not too much to say that the increase of population in the diocese was 25,000 or 26,000 souls a year. He pointed out that the various orYanisations which there were for the increase of the number of clergy in , this diocese had not sufficient power, even if they caught up ;the arrears of population to provide that steady increase ot ! clergy which was absolutely necessary to enable the church to do her work, and that at present the Additional Curates' Society was not in a position to do its share in the work. In this diocese 62 parishes supported the society, 49 pitishes supported the sister society, in 12 parishes they returned, as ' a reason for not helping, that the congregation supported their own curate, 63 declined to give any help whatever from various reasons or from local circumstances To do the work put upon the society required an increase of funds at the , present moment of £1,200 a year. To get that amount with the preient system was impossible, and he suggested the forrnatiqn of a local corn- mittee.—The Right Rev. CHAIRMAN, in addressing the meeting, said in proportion to their population there was not a single diocese in the whole of England and Wales ' which was so badly off for clergy as the diocese of Liver- pool. The population was something like 1,200,000, and

At; INCORRIGIBLE Asirrow GIRL.—At the Wigan County Police Court last Friday, Ellen Pritchard, a young girl, was summoned for stealing 401bs. of coal, belonging to john arion, brick manuiaciurer, stubahaW Cross, Ashton. —Police-constable Hudson said that on the 23rd !lit. he saw the girl coming from the prosecutor's brick yard, carry. coals in a bag. He questioned her, and she said she had not been sent for the coals by any-one.—The mother appeared, and said her daughter was in the habit of staying out at night. They did all they could to keep her under proper control, but it was to no purpose.—The Bench cautioned the defendant and dismissed her, but informed the mother that if she appeared again she would be sent to a re- formatory,

A WIFE BEATER PUNISEED.—Before the magistrates at the Wigan County Police Court on Friday last, Caleb Clark, Ashton, was summoned for having assaulted his wife, I Ann Clark.—Complainant gave evidence to the effect that on the 29th September she did not answer a question which her husband put to her, whereupon he :gave her a violent kick, and pinched her on the arm. He had been cruel to her ever since they were married.—Police-constable Adam- son stated that he had frequently known the defendant to ill-use his wife.—Clark said it was family affairs that made him awkward, but ha denied that he kicked his wife.:....ffe was sent to aaol for a month with barcl lAbour. SUNDAY ItOWIDTISM AT ASIITCS.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday last, the following were summoned for being riotous and disorderly at Ashton the previous Sunday :—Henry Lvthgoe, Joseph Sudworth, Jas. Wood, John Lowe, Peter Gromley, Walter Roscoe Wm. Sudworth, John Painter, Peter Wadsworth, George Partington, James Curran, Peter Clark, George Mee, Charles Rosbottom, Thos. Critchley, and John Penuington.—Mr. Stuart appeared for several of the defendants.—Police-constable Adamson said that at eleven o'clock on Sunday morning he was at Low- bank, Ashton, when be heard a great disturbance on the the highway. He went a round-about way to the scene, and found that with the exception of Rosbottom and Ros- coe,the defendants were making use of profane language, shouting, and whistling. There appeared to have been a row about some pigeon flying. The defendants dispersed in several directions when witness made his appearance.— Moat of the defendants disclaimed any connection with the disturbance, and said they were simply taking a walk.—The Bench ordered each defendant to pay costs. "WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
Roma,

the monthly meeting was held at the 1367:4A Alford. Chambers, on Tuesday afternoon. l'resent-a-Mesat's. F. H. Gossage (chairman), Dr. O'Keeffe,%E. Carey, rank- /m.54 T. Handley, Midwood, Wright, Martley, Shuttle- worth, Webster, Sadler, and Kershaw ; Allen (eel), Hig- ginson (surveyor), Dickson (nuisance inepettor). & PETITION /IN INTOLERABLE PCCISANCE IN 'VICTORIA- ROAD. Mr. H. D. Stringer and Mr. Matthews appeared as a deputaticm, and presented the follsewing petition:— To the Chairman and members of the Widees Local Board. Reptemiter 28, 1881. Gentiernets,—We, ale undersigned, owners and occupiers of property situate in Victoria-road rind immediate neighbourhood, beg to call your attention to the tact that we have for years been subject to an intolerable naisance, great inconvenience, and darnagit; also the danger to 'smith consequent on such a state of things, namely, the over- Sew of the main sewer. backing up into our cellars and leaving u quantity of sewage matter behind. This occurs upon every beavy fall of rain. We have borne with it in the hope that we 'should have some relief from your drainagescheme ; but having 'been informed that the drainage scheme will not avail us, we 'feel constrained to bring our complaint under your notice. We. fear, should an epidemic break out in the neighbourhood, that we should be e.pecially liable to attack. We therefore pray that you will give our comolaint your early and practical attention. We are, respectfully yours, ‘tc.—Then follow about 20 names. The CHAIRXAN intimated that the petition should have the immediate attention of the Board, and suggested that it had best be referred .to the Health and Sewerage Committee.— Mr. STruNGER-said he believed the members were acquainted with the facts long since, and the occupiers and owners thought the petition would have more force if brought be- fore the Board.--The CHAIRMAN: It is before the Board, and it will have all attention, but it must pass through the usual course.—Mr. STRINGER observed that the inhabitants had suffered from the nuisance for the past seven years.—The CHA/RMAN : You may depend ttpon it the matter will have the attention of the Board, and everything that can he done shall be done.—Mr. STRINGER: That is all we ask.—Mr. MarrnE-ws addressed a few works to the members.—Mr. STRINGER, to impress upon the minds of the members the nature of the nuisance of which the inhabitants com- plained, said a fortnight ago he had his cellar cleaned out, and were Mr. Bigginson, the surveyor, present, he would tell-them that his men removed a good barrowful of sewage meter. Next morning the cellar was in a similar state, and again he had it cleaned, and that day it was again in a state of uncleanliness.—The deputation then withdrew. MR. KERSHAW ON THE APPOINTMENT OF OFFICIALS. In moving the confirmation of the minutes of the special meeting at which Mr. Carr was appointed water engineer, Mr. KERSHAW said he hoped the manner in which this ap- pointment was made would not be a precedent for future appointments. He thought the Gas Committee proceeded in a wrong manner in the appointment, and he should like it to be understood that whenever an appointment was to be made, that every :member should have an opportunity of inspecting the applications, which had not been the case in this appointment. Replying to Mr. Pankhurst, Mr. Kershaw I:aiaid he did not wish his remarks to apply to the appoint- ment of assistant officials.—The minutes were passed. MR. BEASLEY ASKING FOR MORE. The following letter was read : Great Western Railway, General Manager's Office, Padding- tcn Stati^n, London, W., October 6th 1882, Dear sir,—l am very sorry to learn from your letter of the 4th (posted yester- day and received this morning) that my letter was too late for your committee. Under those circumstances I shall be obliged if you will endeavour to get me a cheque for £5O or £lOO, on account, at the meatiog of your board, which I tinders'and is to be held next week. I have special reasons for asking for it, and as the matter has been so long in hand altogether, it is not an unreasonable request. lam writing to your chairman to the same effect.—Yours Ac., A. BEASLEY.— J. T. Allen, Esq. The CILLIRSIAN : I may tell you that I have a letter addressed to me, not as chairman of the Board, but as F. H. Gossage, and marked most particularly private all over. (Laughter.) How I am to consider this to be written to the chairman of the Board, Ido not know. However, it is sirrsly repeating what he has written to Mr. Allen privately, and given him permission to make public.—The CLERIC: He has sent me a private letter, which he says I may submit to the Board.—The CHAIRMAN: He doesn't tell you what the urgency is. I think the letter ought to be referred to the Finance Committee.—Mr. MinwooD : The urgency is to get hold of the cheque. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Beasley had also sent a telegram, in Which he asked that if any question of routine stood in the way of his letter being submitted to the Board, they would oblige him by setting it aside.—The communication was referred to the Finance Committee. GAS COMMITTEE. The Gas Committee recommended that the public lamps be charged at the rate of £2 7s. 6d. per lamp, from the Ist April, 1882. That the Widnes Alkali Co., Limited, be offered the use of the lower rooms of the gas offices for £3O per annum, they to pay proportion of rates and do all necessary alterations, and subject to 12 months' notice on either side.—The Water Engineer reported that there were 7,041,913 gallons of water in stock on the 20th ult. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 1616 candles. The wages required during the coming five weeks amounted to £275 for as works and £125 for water works. A. letter had been received from Mr. Deacon, engineer to the Liverpool waterworks, suggesting that the providing of a branch of the Vyrnsvy main for Widnes be left over. The committee recommended that the engineer be instructed to ask that the branch be now pro- vided, or that otherwise the Corporation of Liverpool undertake to do the work when required, at their own expense. A letter, dated the 21st September, was read from Mr. D. Jones, who stated that, through the boring done by the Board, the well supplying his house was now of no use. He asked, therefore, for a supply of water free of cost. The committee recommended that the water be supplied upon the usual terms. Mr. J. F. Allen wrote asking the terms on which t gas and water would be supplied to a new works at Ditton. Lt... The surveyor was instructed to negotiate and obtain in- formation as to the probable requirements of the works. a. The complaint of Mr. Midwood with regard to stop cocks and boxes was considered, but the committee did not see um their way to make any alteration. A letter dated the 21st crae ult. was read from the Widnes Alkali Company offering £3O mar for the use of the whole of the building excepting the Off ground floor offices west of the main entrance, or £4O for the MP whole building for a term of five years certain and twelve all months' notice on either side. The committee recommended ra"M :Oa that the offer of £3O be accepted; an agreement to be entered ay, into.—Mr. HANDLF.Y moved, and Mr. WEBsrER seconded, - - the adoption of the minutes, which motion was passed.— Mr. PAM:C=ST moved, and Mr. HANDLEY seconded, a resolution engaging Mr. Husband, solicitor, to draw up the agreement with the Alkali Co.—Mr. WRIGHT moved that Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., of Warrington, be engaged.— Mr. MsowooD seconded.—Only the mover and seconder voted for the amendment, and the original motion was therefore carried.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

The Highway Committee gave instructions for new lamps to be fixed at the following places :—Bracket lamps: Corner of Salisbury and Hibbert-streets ; Back Passage, Kent-street; opposite end of Thorpe-street; Primitive Methodist Chapel, Princes-street; and corner of Gladstone and Salisbury- streets. Pillar lamps: Corners of Widnes-road and Gladstone- street, and of Albert-road and Kent-street; Appleton footpath, opposite end of Kent-street, easterly end ofJohn-street ; and Widnes-road, opposite Milton Church. Instructions were also given to make the following alterations :—The lamp in John-street to be placed at the corner of John-street and Widnes-road; that at the corner of Widnes-road and Ribbert-street to be placed at the corner of Widnes-road and Travis-street; and that at the junction of Thorpe-street and Dickson-street to be removed from the south-east to the

south-west corner.—The offer of £75 by Messrs. Greenall and Co. be accepted as part payment of the proposed expen- diture with regard to the Mersey Ferry approach.—Mr. W. H. Duggan wrote complaining of the state of the footpath from Simm's Cross to Appleton, and the Surveyor was in- structed to ask-Messrs. Greenall and Co. to repair.—The plans of a house and shop in Salisbury-street, for Mr. J. Phillips, and a house in Oakland-street, for Mr. J. Deacon, were approved.—Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley, solicitors, wrote stating that unless Mr. Mather's claim of £292 131 6d, with respect to Moss Bank Bridge, was settled within seven dlys legal proceedings wou'd be taken for recovery.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. KERSHAW.
MR. SADLER ON CHARITY.

The minutes of the Hospital Committee stated that in- structions ha a been given to the Surveyor to call upon Mr. Sutcliffe to carry out his contract with respect to a copper cylinder. Miss Downie having reported the want of a dining- NOM table for the convalescent room, it was resolved that Mr. Sadler's offer to see about providing one, to cost about 505., be accepted.—Mr. SADLER moved, and Mr. JOHNSON seconded the passing of the minutes.—Mr. Mmwoop re- marked that he understood the hospital was thoroughly fitted up, and he really should like to know how it was that the cylinder and table were required after all the money that had been expended on the place.—Mr. SADLER replied that the cylinder had not been fixed up according to agree- ment made some time ago. With regard to the table, he supposed it could notbe reasonably expected that Mr. Mid- wood would sanction the spending of £2 Ios. without offer- ing up a protest against it. In this instance he thought Mr. Midwood ought to be more charitable. The things were for a good cause, and if Mr. Midwood would only consider that "charity covers a multitude of sins" he would be more charitable. The convalescent ward was without a table, and when patients were recovering and in that room' there was not a place where a cup of tea could be placed before them. The minutes were passed. WAY LEAVE. —RESIDENT OFFICIALS. At a meeting of the sewerage Committee on the 2nd October, 1882, the resident Engineer reported that the pro- gress of the sewerage work comprised by this contract had been satisfactory during the past month. The contractor had commenced the excavation on the south side of the Viaduct, and was now ready to mako a start with the brick- work. The amount due to the contractor for the month ending September 20th was £363 149 Id. Mr. Jeffreys had received £127 lOs 11d, and Mr. Kirk £321 8s 10d. These items amounted to £Bl2 13s 10,1,the total for work done under this contract to September 20th, 18112.—Letters were read from Messrs. Part and Co., solicitors, declining to leave the question of wayleave thtough Hutchinson's trustees' land to a single arbitrator to be appointed by the Local Government Board.—Mr. KERSHAW proposed that the minutes be passed. The Board would see that Messrs. Hutchinson bad declined to accept the Local Government Board arbitrator in the matter, and the inference was that they would appoint Mr. Torning. The Board ought at an early day appoint a gentleman to meet Mr. Turning. The Board had had two or three recommendations, viz.: Mr. Linaker, of Frodsham, a gentleman of great experience in these matters; Mr.

Wilson, of St. Helets •, and Mt Hanson, who was recom- mended to the Board by the ;Sewerage Committee.—These were the three gentlemen Denied, but he believed Mr. Linaker was the be for the work. Mr. Midwood would say some- , thing either for Mr. Ihnaker or on the subject.—Mr. Mm- WOOD: I have nothing to say on that sublect, KEUSHAW thought the matter ought to be brought to a =min- SADLEtt asked the meaning of the phrase "resident engineer," and said the Board had too many officers residing I out of the town. He thought it was time the Board took some stand about officers living in the district.—Mr. KER- SHAW : Perhaps you would have to do something with the members residing out of the district. (Laughter.)—The CRAiname: I most heartily wish you would.—The minutes { were then confirmed. THE MEDICAL OFFICER AND HIS The minutes of the Health Committee contained the Medical Officer's report, which stated that daring September there had been 81 births and 44 deaths, representing a birth rate of 38-88 per 1,000, and a death-rate of 21.12 pr 1,000. Of the deaths 1.5 were children under one year, and 15 children between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused 12. The Nrisance Inspector stated six new cases of scarlet fever had been reported, lout as there were no deaths during the month he considered the disease wasl declining. Disinfection had been attended to. Notices had been served upon Mr. Urquhart and Mr. Midwood, on behalf of the railway company, to abate ngisances caused through pig keeping. The committee recommended Mr. Urquhart be allowed a month or six weeks to abate the nuisance; and that a further notice be given to Mr. Midwood, that unless the nuisance was abated by the 10th inst. proceedings would be taken. Messrs. Cash and Davies hiving complained as to the state of their cellar, the surveyor was instructed to see the owners of the property, and also of that adjoining, and ask if they will contribute a proportion of the cost of extending the sewer in Lugsdale-road. Recommended that Mr. William Cooper be re-appointed medical officer of health •for the 12 months ending October, 1883, at his I present salary, £6O per annum. The receipts from the Market for September amounted to £27 12s id, including £l4 143 from the Fair Ground. The fair had only -Produced about one-half of the amount of the one held last autumn. Five shops were now let and the stalls were letting better. Recommended that the pig pens at the market be boarded up at a cost of not exceeding 255. Recommended that the regulation as to the half-mile radius be suspended, and that in future all persons hawking tollable goods within the Board's district be compelled to pay a toll at the rate of is. per day or 3s. per week, 10s. permonth, and 20s. per quarter.—Mr. CAREY moved, and Dr. O'KEEFFE seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. SA.DLER asked if it was intended that the I medical officer should be present at the Board's meetings.— Mr. MIDWOOD, referring to the notice to.be served upon him, said it was now the 10th of the month, and the summons had not vet arrived. How then could he abate the nuisance within the time mentioned? He also wished to know if it was stated in the appointment of the medical officer, that that gentleman was to attend the Board's meeting. The salary was sufficient to require kim to attend.—Mr. WEBSTER wished to be informed of what had been done with the carcase of a diseased pig which heti been seized.—Mr. CAREY, replying to Mr. Sadler, said Mr. Cooper was willing to attend the meetings if the Board desired his attendance, but the committee thought it unnecessary. At one time he did attend, and sat in the room all the afternoon, and never a question was asked him. The pig inquired about by Mr. Webster, he supposed, was destroyed in the usual way at the gas works, where Mr. Dickson had all the necessary apparatus fixed. Mr. Dickson sometimes buried the pigs, and he should fancy he used some of the fat for the wheels of the Board's carts. (Laughter.)—Mr. WEBSTER thought the pigs ought to be buried, and net turned into profit.—Mr. CAREY, speaking with reference to Mr. Mid- wood's remarks, said a notice was served upon him as a representative of the railway company in this particular instance, on the 21st September, asking him to abate the nuisance. The nuisance was not abated, and at the commit- tee meeting, it was resolved that nuisance must be abated by the 10th. It appeared that Mr. Allen had not served the latter notice.—Mr. MIDWOOD said the company were pre- pared to drain or sewer any premises where they could find a nuisance existed.—The CF SIMIAN remarked that he had seen the medical officer attend six or seven Board meetings and never been asked a question ; or had anything to say or do, but sit there the entire time of the meeting, and the meetings used to last a great length of time then.—Mr. SADLER : I should think he got his money easily if he did that.—Mr. CAREY: That is not what he gets paid for. He has to look after the health of the town and I should think it is a waste of time to come and sit down there instead of looking after his business out of doors.—The minutes were passed.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended that the followieg accounts be paid :—Gas, £345 17s 9d; water, £lB6 15s 61; Highway Committee,E73 is 3d; hospital, £2B 13s; sewerage, £3BO 7s 5d ; health, £95 16s 3d; market, £7 13s id; finance, £Bll 9s 3J; Jane Davies, £l,OOl 4s. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Handley, econded by Mr. Midwood.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
OFFICERS' DUTIES.

Same time ago the Highway and Sanitary Committee was deputed by the Board to consider the advisability of re- arranging the duties and salaries of the officials of the Board. The committee, in its turn, delegated the mdtter to a sub-committee, which, on Thursday afternoon last, pre- sented the following report to the committee :—" Ist. That Mr. Brooks' salary and duties remain as heretofore. 2. That Mr. Barker's salary remain as heretofore, and that his duties be increased, he taking the whole of the inspector of nuisances and other work carried out by James Parry with ' the exception of the inspection and registration of lodging houses and canal boats. 3. That Mr. Dutton's salary be in- creased £lO per annum,- and in addition to his own duties, he takes charge of the inspection told registration of lodging houses, and to have an assistant for a few hours during two days per week at a cost of not more than 3s. per week. Also that Mr. Boot be appointed canal boat inspector at a salary of £lO per annum, and that he presents a report to the committee each month." The report was adopted by the committee, and a special meeting of the Board was afterwards held for the purpose of confirm- ing the proposal. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Norman, W. Fisher, W. H. Lightbourne, J. J. Speakman, P. Briscoe; W, Lake, P. Speakman, Taylor, J. Meadowcroft, W. H. Linaker (law • clerk), and W. H. Brookes (secretary). On the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. P. SPEAKMAN, the report was adopted, after a technical objection by Mr. Lake had been overruled by the Chairman.

div.head: SHOCKING STREET ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. THE INQUEST.
div.p: SHOCKING STREET ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. THE INQUEST.

A street accident of a shocking nature occurred at the junction of Wareing-street and Lugsdale-road, on Tuesday evening. A boy named Richard Christopher Tobin, six years of age, was riding behind a lurry which was crossing Lugsdale-road, when a cart belonging to Mr. W illiam Gallop, of Warrington, came along and knocked the deceased to the ground. The wheels of the cart passed over the head of the poor boy, whose brains were scattered in the road. He was conveyed home and Dr. O'Keeffe sent for. When the doctor arrived, however, he was dead.

Yesterday, the county coroner, Mr. C. E. Driffield, held an inquest on the body at the Market Hotel. John Tobin, labourer at Messrs.Gaskell, Deacon and Co.'s chemical works, said he lived in Wareing-street, off Lugs- dale-road. The deceased was his son, and about six years of age. The accident occurred about five o'clock on Tues- day evening, and when he (witness) arrived home from work he found his boy lying on the table dead. He did not attri- bute blame to anyone. John Bleakly, joiner, of 21, Victoria-road, Widnes, deposed that on Tuesday afternoon, between half-past four and five o'clock, he was in Lugsdale-road, when he saw a lurry coming hown. The driver was riding with reins. Behind the lurry, hanging on by an iron bar, was the dnesed and another boy. The lurry turned down Vice-street, and was followed by several other lurries. As it turned down the street the two boys dropped off the lurry At this moment a gingerbeer cart, proceeding in the direc- tion of Warrington, came up the road. One of the boys fell on his back en the ground, but the deceased got in the way of the cart, and was knocked down and run over. He fell under the right-hand wheel of the cart, which passed over his bead.
By the Coroner: Both drivers appeared to be sober. They did not seem to have seen the lads, and so far as he (wit- ness) could see, no one was to blame for the accident. _ _

Inspector Barnett said both drivers went to the police office and reported the matter immediately after it occurred. Both were perfectly sober. Edwin Thompson' of 7, Dials-court, said he was driver of a cart belonging to Mr. Wm. Gallop, gingerbeer manufac- turer, Warrington. On Tuesday he had served his customers in Widnes, and was returning home by Lugsdale-road, when a lurry crossed the road for the purpose of proceeding down Vine-street. He heard Bleakly shout, and felt the cart give a lurch. At once he stopped it, and found the deceased under the wheel. The boy was dead. He was bleeding from the head, and his brains were scattered on the road. Mr. Sadler, a juryman, said Thompson had given his evidence iu a satisfactory way, and the jury generally con- curred in approving of the action of Thompson. The Coroner remarked that the jury might say the occur- rence was purely accidental, and the jury returned a verdict accordingly.
