div.head: r TIIE EXAMINER SA.IkII,DAY, OCTOBER 14, 1882.4
div.p: r TIIE EXAMINER SA.IkII,DAY, OCTOBER 14, 1882.4
THE ALPINE CHOIR.

TEMPERANCE MEETING. Professor Andrei Alpine choir, who have given enter- tainments in the Warrington Public Hall during the past week, gave their farewell concert on Tuesday evening. to a trowde& audience. The object of Professor Andre le tto provide healthy entertainments for the people, and that his efforts in this direction have been successful, has been demonstrated by the large audiences which have assembled at the hall since the per- formances of his choir became known. As has been previ- ously stated, the entertainments partake of a sacred and secular character, and the whole tendency of the latter is to inculcate the importance of in tegrityand total abstinence. With the object of promoting the temperance cause, a meeting vas held on Wednesday evening under the presidency of Mr. R. Naytor, who was supported by the Rev. W. Mules, the Rev. T. Rippon, Professor Andre, Messrs. R. Garnett, R. Roberts, T. Flood, R. Siddall, J. W. Hall, and W. Roberts. The usual programme of songs, choruses, and recitations was ably given, much to the delight of the audience, who redemanded almost every piece. In opening the meeting, The CHAIRMAN remarked that he felt sure they would wish in their hearts that the .chairman as well as the other speakers that night would be very witty, and ob- serve what Shakespeare once said about witticism—that "brevity is the soul of wit "—(hear, hear,—for he felt certain they had come for the purpose of listening to the sweet music and to the recitations to be given by the choir which Prof. Andre had ,brought into the town. (Ap- plause.) He did not know that it was really necessary for any speeches at all to be made, for he guessed that most of them sympathised with the object of that gather- ing, and were ip harmony with the efforts now being put forth in different parts of the country for the furtherance of their object, the furtherance of true sobriety. From the number of invitations he had received lately to attend large demonstrations of that description in different parts of the district, he thought they might come to the con- clusion that there was at the present time a kind of rustling amongst the dry bones, and a thorough determination in the hearts of many to do more than they had been accustomed to do in the past for the furtherance of this great and good work. He thought there was one thing that they should always avoid, and that was using harsh language. (Hear, hear.) sometimes they had been a little remiss in that respect, and instead of furthering the object that they had in view they had damaged the cause very ma- terially. It had been said upon many occasions that moderate drinkers were worse than drunkards. Some peeple thought that a very uncharitable observation. The moderate drinker might turn round and say that the teetotaller was worse than the drunkard, and he dared say the moderate drinker would have a great amount of justification for making such an amirtioß, for he believed there were many teetotallers who were really worse than drunkards. Teetotalism was not everything, and, though they might have the advantage in that particular respect, they might be guilty of other sins of which the drunkard was free; so that if they were placed in the balances of justice, the drunkard in this instance might have the advantage. Not that drunken- ness made a man better or that teetotalism made a man worse, but take a man all round, and he thought they might find even teetotallers who were worse than moderate drinkers, aud worse than some drunkards. Let them place themselves in the drunkard's position. They condemned the vice of drunkenness; but they should always have an amount of pity for the poor drunkard. If they or he had been sur- rounded by the same circumstances and brought up under the same influences, where would they have been that day? They might have been grovelling lower in the mire than the drunkard whom they would condemn. Let them be very careful about the wholesale condemnation that they bad been accustomed to deal out to those who could not see eye to eye with them. In some respects they might be infinitely better, but one thing he would say, and it was this: that good as they were, they would be better still if they would go and join the ranks of total abstainers. (Applause). He did not suppose that it was necessary for him to say much more to them. He was very glad to see such a very large gathering that night. It clearly demonstrated that the sympathies of the people were awakening to the good cause that they were met together for the purpose of furthering by that entertainment; and he trusted that the result would be that some of the audience who had not yet quite seen eye to eye with them would be convinced that night that teetotallers were on the safest and best side, and would come round to the table and sign the pledge. (Applause). Let them carry on this temperance work with more Christian charity. They might depend upon it if they did, they would make greater headway. They had just about kept pace with the growth of population in the country in the past, and he thought if they could only get these good-hearted ladies and gentlemen to come forward and join them, and if they would all work right willingly there was not the least doubt the next few yeers would see a decided change in the public opinion of this country in reference to those customs and practices of society which sanction the use of intoxicating liquors. Let them do all they possibly could for the furtherance of this great work, knowing that they had received themselves so many rich blessings from it. What might they have been that day if it had not been for total abstinence? They had nothing to boast of. No man had much righteousness of his own; in fact, what little goodness they might possess Flight have been granted to them not by what they had done themselves, ' but through the intercession of the righteous, some of whom still lived amongst them, and some of whcm had been taken hence. Let them be determined— for they had not very long to live at ths longest—that they. would lean what little influence they had on the side of truth and of righteousness; and if they laboured for the pros- perity and weal of the country and its inhabitants, if they did this from right and pure motives, what would the result be? They might not gain the approbation of those by whom they were surrounded, but he would promise them that-they would be amply repaid by having a sweet satisfaction in their souls which was akin to that "peace of mind which passeth all understanding," and which those. only were in possession of who were determined to do what was right in the sight of God and man. (Applause.) Labour on, their reward would be sure, and as they came to the close of life's journey, if they had been faithful to their Maker they would see those golden gates, and the welcome would be given to them from its pearly portals,and they would pass into that land where they would see the King in His beauty and which even now might not be very far off. (Loud ap- plause. After reading a letter of apology for non-attendance from the Rev. John Yonge, the CHAIRMAN called upon Mr. R. GARNETT, who said the temperance movement had the heartest sympathy of himself, of, he believed, every one on the platform, and he believed of none mere so than Professor Andre—(hear, hear)—who had devoted a large portion of his time and a very considerable amount of money derived from similar meetings to that to spread temperance throughout the length and breadth of the land. (Applause.) The benevolence of Professor Andre was quite sufficient to stamp him in their estimation as a man who deserved to be esteemed and hononred. He believed in brevity, and con- cluded by stating that the temperance cause had his best I wishes. (Applause.) ; The Rev. W. MULES said he was very proud to stand I upon that platform that night for more reasons than one. He was proud to stand upon the platform with such a man as Professor Andre—(applause)—and with such a company as the company of singers there. He had often longed to go to Switzerland. He had wanted to see the beautiful Alps, but now he wanted to go there to see the Swiss people, for if they were all like Professor Andre he was sure they must be worth going to see and going to hear, if for nothing else. He was very proud and very happy because the platform was filled with representatives of different branches of the Church of Christ who had met together that night, and with one voice, to raise the cry of war against the great drink Send of our land, or rather to sustain the cry which had already been raised. He was firmly convinced in:his own mind that, whatever others might say, the drink fiend was the most furious and the most deadly fiend— (hear, hear)—not only of oar own land but of our common race. He believed that the evil of intemperance, more effectually than any other, destroyed the last vestiges of God's image in the heart of man, and reduced him to the lowest level of the brute creation. (Applause.) The effect of all sin, as he understood it, was to make man less like God and more like the devil. The covetous man wrote that for himself upon every object which his greedy eyes rested upon, and with self as his motto, he 14gan life and he ended it The man of pride did try to gain for himself admiration in the world; but the poor drunkard, under the influences of a passion over which he had no control whatever, reeled through life and staggered into the grave with this label affixed on his brow :—" Myself, my family, and all that I have for the grave and destruction." (Applause.) When he went into the house of a man who, though he were a great sinner, strove to make his home happy, and had a look of love for his children,and a word of encouragement for his wife, and strove to throw a circle of gladness around his fireside, there he saw traces of something better that had been or of something nobler to be. When he went into the house of perhaps a thief, and looked, as a man might look sometimes, through the face of that man into his heart, and saw that the very theft, which he had committed was committed perhaps to hush the cry of his starving children for bread, he saw tracee there of past glory and magnificence, just as they had stood sometimes and looked upon the broken arches and beautiful tracery of some ruined and deserted castle, and thought of the glory and magnificence which once were there, but now were gone. But, when he went into the poor home of the drunkard and listened to the cry of terror which was its only music, and gazed upon its dismantled walls, and looked into its rifled cupboards, and worst of all upon the bloated face of the body which was only the shrine of the fiend, he saw in that a piece of broken tracery which reminded him of past glory, and "Ichabod " seemed to be written upon every inch of the man—body and soul. (Applause.) It was that then that made him -glad that night that the ' Christian Church had at last agreed to acknowledge, or per- haps he had better say had been fosced to acknowledge, that the evil of intemperance was the greatest enemy of the re- ligion of Jesus Christ. (Applause.) Too long, alas, had the Church of God slumbered and slept whilst thousands of their fellow-creatures poured forth the despairing cry "No man cares for our souls." Sad, indeed, had it been to see,—sad enough to make angels weep, and men to tremble, to see Christian men and Christian women in their luxurious homes sitting down in lazy indolence, and in guilty indifference drinking the old : draught" Am I my brother's keeper ? " Too long, alas, had they drunk that, but now, thank God, that platform told them of better and brighter days. It told them that the Christian church had at last become aroused to a sense of her duty. It told them that the old dose so long and so often administered had lost its composing

power, its semniferous influence; and now Christians of every sha4c of opinion, Christians of every religious de- nomination, were rising to- one cry—Death to the drink fiend, the greatest enemy to our land and to the Christian Church. (Applause). That was the burden of their cry to every Christian man and to every Christian woman pre- sent. Come and rally round their standard. They had up- lifted it, and might heaven's breezes shake out every fold, co that their motto "No surrender " might be seen by their enemies as well as by their friends. They had begun the fight; they would -sustain the fight; and by and by, God helping them, victory would he theirs. (Loud applause). Mr. T. FLOM next addressed the meeting, and impressed upon the audience their du'y in respect to the temperance cause. Professor ANDRE, who followed, thanked them for their kind reception of his -choir, and stated that before he came to England he was a temperance man; but when he cime to this country he found it necessary to become a total abstainer. The CHAIRMAN said he thought Professor Andre deserved not only the thanks of the people of Warrington, but the country at large, for his efforts in support of the temperance movement. The Rev. T. RIPPON was present that night to show his sympathy with Professor Andr6 in the work he had at heart, and the work he was doing in endeavouring to promote healthy entertainments for the masses. (Hear, hear.) He thought that was one thing that certainly was needed in our towns and in our country to-day. He was also present to sympathise with the object which, as a Blue Rihboner, he had at heart, viz., the temperance cause. There were many things in Warrington that they wanted. They wanted healthier entertainments for the people. They wanted better houses for the poor people, and they wanted fewer public houses. He was thankful to know, after havingconversation with some in authority in the town, that the magistrates of Warrington had sympathy with that movement, that they were anxious to help temperance, and he hoped that the temperance men of Warrington would stand by the magistrates in this particular. There was, undoubtedly, rolled over the country a wave of gospel sentiment. A friend, who had just come from the city, told him the other day the city seemed to be affected with the blue, as nearly every second man and woman he met wore the blue ribbon. In Spurgeon's Tabernacle a glorious Blue Ribbon mission had been conducted by Mr. R. T. Booth ; many thousands had donned the" blue." At the Wesleyan conference many ministers he saw wore the "bit of blue," whilst last week in Liverpool at the Baptist Union the same thine' was noticeable. Let them thank God for the signs of the times. He was sure if they had in War- rington a mission like they had last spring, which was most successful, it would be marked with the same success, if only they set themselves to do it. In the words of Burke to his constituents " Applaul us when we run, console us when we fall, cheer us when we rise, but above all things let us go on, for God's sake let us go on." (Applause.) The entertainment concluded with Herr Klein's truly wonderful representation of the bombardment of Alexandria.

THE TWENTY-FIRST L SHAM FIGHT AT ST. HELENS. On Saturday afternoon a sham fight, on a small scale, was held near St. Helens, for the purpose of practising the members of the above corps in defence and attack move- ments. The scene of operations was the fields which lie between Moss Bank station and Windle Hall, the residence of Major W. W. Pilkington, the latter place being the ob- ject defended. The ground selected was admirably adapted for the purpose in view, as Windle Hall, looked at from the I base of attack, is situated on a commanding eminence and I though its defensive capabilities are somewhat lessened by an open space in front, yet by pushing forward the defenders were able to secure possession of some clumps of trees and hedges, and a small brook in their front was a further im- pediment to the advance of their opponents. On the other hand the attacking, whose base was Moss Bank station, were favoured in making their preliminary movements by high hedges and a road which almost encircled the scene of operations. The attacking party, which consisted of 13 officers, 17 sergeants, 22 band and buglers, and 187 rank and file from the Prescot, Widnes, and Sutton companies, under the command of Major W. W. Pilkington, Major White, with Lieutenant D. Gamble, jun., acing as aide-de- camp, were conveyed shortly after three o'clock to Moss Bank railway station. About the same time the defending party, which consisted of 11 officers, 11 sergeants, 24 band and buglers, and 156 rank and file—all belonging to the St. Helens companies—under the command of Lieut.-Colonel Gamble, Major R. Pilkington, and Major and Adjutant Wilcocks, arrived at Windle Hall by road. Colonel H. J. Bell, com- manding the Bth and 40th regimental districts (Warrington), with Lieutenant and Adjutant R. H. Hall, as aid-de-camp, was present throughout the proceedings. The attack was commenced by Major Pilkington' throwing the Prescot and Sutton companies into the fields immediately in front of the station, and deploying them as skirmishers The Pre- scot company which was on the extreme left advanced through a turnip and potatoe field down into the hollow, but were there met by a strong body of defenders, who, after the expenditure of a prodigious amount of blank cartridge, drove them back again into the turnip field, where the aggressors made a valiant stand, and ultimately compelled the defending party to retire back to their original position. In the meantime the Sutton company which occupied what might be termed a central position kept up a lively fire— without, however, advancing—on the defenders, whose fusillade was of an equally lively character, and, being under better shelter, naturally had the best of the encounter. The turning paint, however, in favour of the attack, was made by a clever strategic movement on the part of the commander, in advancing the Widnes company, which had hitherto remained in reserve, round to the right. They were there enabled to take up a remarkably well sheltered posi- tion on the flank of the defenders, who had but indifferent shelter at this point. This advantage was further utilised by the Prescot company being drawn away from the left to strengthen the Widnes company. The defenders op- posed to these two companies made an obstinate stand, but were at length compelled to fall back, closely followed by the assailants. Under favour of this effective diversion, the Sutton company was enabled to make a vigorous advance on what was now the left of the attack, and finally, by a gallant rush, they crossed ,the stream and drove the defenders opposed to them from their sheltered position into the open ground. A grand advance was now made from all sides by the attacking party, who drove the defenders in upon each other at the foot of the slope immediately in front of the hall. "Cease firing" was then ordered, and the battalion was drawn up and ad- dressed by Col. BELL, who said he had enjoyed himself that evening very much indeed, and, therefore, he thought it right to tell them so. It had given him a great deal of plea- sure in coming there to see the way they performed the at- tack, and he would also say the defence. They had had as excellent ground to move upon as they could wish for— plenty of water, wood, and elevated ground—and, therefore, he was not surprised that it had turned out to be a very creditable engagement. But there were one or two things, however, which he should like to point out to them so that, in case they should repeat the movements they might guard against them in future. He had noticed a company—which company it was he could not say, but the captain would know—of which half a section, at the commencement of the engagement, was standing up in the middle of a potato field —if they had been in action they would soon have been lying down. (Laughter.) There was another time he saw— he was not finding fault with them, but only pointed these things out that they might guard against them in future— another company on the right of the attack, which if he had been umpire he should have put out of the engagement altogether, and then the tables would have been turned— instead of the attacking party being there the defenders would have taken their ground. That would have really been the case, as he saw the company going across without taking advantage of the shelter of the different hedges and different roads. It would have been much better had they gone along the road instead of across the open field, and thus taken advantage of the different shelters. He had no other remarks to make, and he thought the whole affair had been very creditable and very instructive for all. (Ap- plause.)—Colonel GlaißLx then addressed the battalion, and said he hoped they all felt that that day bad given them some instruction and some7pleasure—he thought it ought to have given them both. They were all very much indebted to Colonel Bell for coming over to assist them in their manoeuvres, They did not often get an opportunity of doing so much as they had done that day, and it was a great advantage to have Colonel Bell there. He was very sorry that they had had so small a :Truster. Out of a corps of 800 they had only got 444 present. There might be some explanation for the small attendance which he had not yet got, but as it was he thought they had done tolerably well. There were some things Colonel Bell had not mentioned. At the left of the attack there were six men who remained behind after their company had been moved away, but these men should have retired altogether, and then the company opposed to them could also have retired, which was neces- sary to carry out the remainder of the programme. They should not carry on warfare on their own hook. but only under command of the officer who commanded their company. Col. Gamble then concluded by expressing

div.head: MR. BRIGHT AND THE REV. T. RIPPON.
div.p: MR. BRIGHT AND THE REV. T. RIPPON.

Mr. Bright has sometimes been disrespectfully spoken of as "an old figure-head." The term was not used in the loose sense in which cabmen and other humourists in the streets employ it, but with a precise significance. Our con- temporary the Spectator, though a Liberal, is a spirited organ, and is at all times ready to call on the Ryots, the Baboos, the Blieesties, and the Hookabadhars, to rally round the standard .of England. Consequently the Spectator ventured to observe that Mr. Bright "did not oppose the Egyptian war in particular, but all wars." It follows that Mr. Bright must, when a Gladstonian war arises, frequently be in opposition to the Spectator, and therefore to all thoughtful Christian men who read John Iraglesant and worship the Premier. Now there is in Warrington a thought- ful Christian Ulan, Mr. Rippon, a Wesleyan minister, whose conscience was sorely tried by the dif- ferences in the Liberal party. Here on one side was Mr. Gladstone ordering bombardments and horrid personally conducted charges with the naked bayonet. Here was the Spectator backing him, and thinking, as engaged men—according to the elder Mr. Weller—think of matrimony, that it " wos all wery cipital." And here, on the other side, was Mr. Bright, who, after tolerating a bombardment, rcr,- volted against war on dry land, and threw up a lucrative and easy position as figure-head in obedience to his con- , science. What was a Wesleyan minister to think? Mr. Gladstone could not be wrong, the Spectator could not be mistaken (especially on a moral question), and yet it was scarcely possible to hold that Mr. Bright could be in error. Mr. Itippon might have founded a Gladstone Society, and put the problem before it. Or he might have done what the Browning Society does when it doubts—he might have written to the author of his puzzle. This course Mr. Rippon chose; he wrote to Mr. Bright, showing that "peace at any price was an untenable position, and that the Egyptian war seemed a righteous one from that stand- point." From what standpoint? However, we are not concerned with Mr. Rippon's grammar, but with Mr. Bright's ideas about the war. Mr. Bright, in a letter to Mr. Rippon, denied that he had ever opposed any war on the ground that all war was immoral. "I have never expressed such an opinion." Indeed we do not know that Mr. Bright ever denounced either the American Civil War or the Russo-Turkish war at all. He generally confines himself to the wars waged by his own country. He has condemned all our poor wars on their merits; we are always in the wrong; whether war "in the aibstrac' " be immoral or not, our wars are invariably immoral. We may fight Chinese or Afghans, Russians, Zulus, or Egyptians, but we, unluckily, can never be in the right.— Saturday Review.

div.head: BATTLE OF TEL-EL-KEBIR.
div.p: THE BATTLE OF TEL-EL-KEBIR.
LETTER FROM AN ASHTON SOLDIER.

The long and interesting communication which follows has been received by Mr. Thomas Winstanley, boot and shoe maker, Ashton, whose son Thomas (the writer) is a private in the No. I. Bearer Column, A.H. Corps, at present serving in Egypt. It might be of some interest to state that other communications have been received from private Winstanley who was present at the battle of Kassassin, and his " mate" while assisting him in carrying a " stretcher" was shot dead. The following letter was delivered on Tues- day evening last, having occupied thirteen days in its transit.

Cairo, September 26th, 1882.-1 am enjoying the best of health, such as the climate allows us, and I am able to do my duty to my fellow-comrades who need it—they, who are dying so far from kindred, friends, and home. What a pleasant task it is. I cannot describe to you the value of my humble services. I never did value myself much until we got into the midst of s'ckness, different sickness to that at home. But now is the time we are called forth to use all our energy, go where you will, do what you will, they are all crying out for the doctor and orderlies. It is a try- ing time without any doubt. The officers are just as bad and as poor as the privates—they are thought no more of. They get to eat the same as we and that is nothing a good many times. I have always had a desire of seeing a battle field, and I have seen one to my heart's content. Never shal I forget one on the night of the 12th of September. We were lying down to go to sleep, when the bugle sounded to "fall in," and in we fell. I should say at that time it was half-past eight. We started, and left -our camp standing. We marched from Kassassin to just outside the enemy's forts, and there waited for daybreak on the 13th. We were told to lie down and sleep for a few hours, but sleep was gone. All we thought about was what was going to follow on the morrow. At three o'clock the whisper went round in the darkness," Get ready every man," Not a man sunk from it. Steadily we went on until four o'clock. Then we were halted for a few minutes to fill our water-bottles with water, then on again. At 5 o'clock we were steadily advancing, and our outpost was attacked. Then we knew the time was come. Our artillery opened fire on them, and as soon as that was done they opened fire on us, and for one hour we did not move an inch. Not a word could you hear; but could see them falling around you, yet not speaking to them. Still keeping up the fire, at last there's a shout "England for ever charge!" and great was the charge for fully an hour and a half. Nothing but the bayonet was used; not a man failed to du his duty. Then they gave way. By this time we are getting up to the forts —they are all entrenched. We are in the open place, and nothing to hide us from the shot and shell; yet we fell not back, but onward steadily advancing until at last the grand and noble charge which will not be forgotten for some time. Up they went in the trenches, knowing at the time it was either life or death, and many can tell the tale of the gallant charge of Tel-el-Kebir. At the time that all this was going on we were close behind with our stretchers ready to pick up the dying and wounded, and from 7 a.m. until 12 p.m., the same night we were on the battle field working all the time—getting off the wounded. We got our wounded off the field the same night—that is all the English—and then it took us four days to get off the Arabs and Egyptians. I don't know whether you heard how many wounded they had on their side. In four days we carried two thousand five hundred off the battle field, and the last day was a day that will not be forgotten by a good many. We had to go and dress their wounds, our nose bandage un to keep out the stench that came from the wounds. What with them and the dead, never could any- one describe it. We got them all in, however, and dressed them, working day and night—not only us but the doctors as well. I had nothing to eat for three days—only drinking at times a little brandy and lime-juice as stimulants to keep up our nerves. We amputated 100 legs and 55 arms; that is, we took them off, and we had to assist in them all, and that lasted until the liith of September, when we got rid of them by handing them over to their own doctors and men. We got all straight, and on the 20th of September started to march to that famous city Cairo. After three days weary march through the plain of Arabia we got in, and I must say a more nobler and more beautiful city no one ever wished to see. We are now stopping in the citadel of Cairo, one of the palaces, waiting for orders to go to that famous city Alexandria, and I think by the time you get this I shall not be very far off; so I think I must finish this letter, as I must up and be doing."

WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CRIIRCII.— After all absence of three weeks recruiting his health, the Rev. John Yonge resumed his duties at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday morning last, and in the evening de- livered an able discourze on the responsibility of minister and congregation in preaching and hearing the gospel.

div.head: LECTURE ON STARR – BOWKETT BUILDING, SOCIETIES.
div.p: LECTURE ON STARR - BOWKETT BUILDING, SOCIETIES.

On Wednesday evening, a lecture was delivered in the Assembly Room of the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens, by Ed. J. Collings, Esq., of Bolton, subject: "The aims, objects, prin- ciples, and working of Srarr-Bowkett Building Societies." The chair was taken by Mr. G. Webster, who, in intro- ducing the lecturer, remarked that he took the chair that evening with great pleasure; the Starr-Bowkett Societies encouraged a man to use the word "thrift" in a right way, to put it to a practical, honest, and manly use. These , societies enabled a working man to put a little of his hard earnings on one side in order, eventually, to save his rent and have a house of his own. Thus they encouraged thrift and self-respect. He might aid that he knew some little of the working classes ; he had watched them in their trials, in their struggling to get on, in their poverty and affliction, and could fully appreciate the great assistance they might derive towards bettering themselves from societies like these. He then called upon the lecturer, Mr. Collings, who in a very interesting and thoughtful lecture dealt with the general question of thrift aud the various plans for its encouragement. Referring ft) the facili- ties offered by tlle Postal authorities for saving by means of stamps, the lecturer urged upon all parents the importance of encouraging their children to save in this way, urging that the result in after life would certainly be found in thrifty citizens. The lecturer also drew atten- tion to the plan recently adopted by the Go- vernment by which any person having 10 can become an investor in the Government stocks. In ex-. plaining the Starr-Bowkett Societies' plan, the lecturer said it was not his business to attack permanent building socie- ties; they were very good for the people they were intended for, but the Starr-Bowkett societies reached a class which they eould not touch. A Starr-Bowkett society consisted of 500 members, each of whom might have one, two, three, four, or any number of shares. When a member entered the society he was given a certain number, which was called his register number, and under which he might have one, two, three, or four shares only. If the member took eight shares he would have two register numbers. The effect of this was that the society could never be called upon for more than £4OO at any one time. A person could enter the society at any age, and thus parents could take up shares for their children when quite young, and the impression caused on the child's mind by the parents thus saving for it would in- variably prove a barrier to that child's ever going wrong; besides which, if the shares were appropriated before the child left home, the parent would be able to point to the house bought with the appropriation money, and in this way the bonds of parental affection would be greatly increased. The subscriptions were 6d. per week on each £lOO share, calculated to run for 21 years, though as a matter of fact the societies never run that length of time, making alto- gether the sum of £27 6s to be subscribed on each share. Every so often the members were called together to make an appropriation. If a member had taken say four shares, and was fortunate in the ballot, he would become entitled to an advance of £4OO, free of interest, for 12i years. A member would not be entitled to the appropriation if he was not clear on the books, and this rule brought people into the habit of paying regularly and punctually. The member having gained his appropriation' either uses it in buying property or sells his right to it as he pleases. If he sold, he would be able to get a price, varying with the demand, of from £4O to £7O. The appropriation money had to be spent in buy- ing property, when the society would advance upon it the full commercial value which:from the peculiar constitution of the society they were perfectly safe in doing. The mem- ber then began to repay the amount at the rate of £8 per cent. per annum, and at the end of 121 years he would have paid off the £4OO out of the rents of the property. The lecturer further illustrated at length the working and prin- ciples of the societies. The accumulated subscriptions were lent out to the members in turn free.of interest, and on the other hand no interest was paid by the society for the sub- scriptions themselves; the principles: were purely those of co-operation, while the working expenses were met by a small charge of is. 3d. per share per annum. In conclu- sion he expressed his conviction that all who joined these societies would become active agents in disseminating these principles amongst those by whom they were surrounded. (Applause).—At the conclusion of the lecture the eighth appropriation of the Second St. Helens (350th) Starr-Bow- kett Building Society was made, the successful member being Mr.' J. B. Rose, of Church-street and Market-street, St. Helens, confectioner, who, having two shares under register No. 358, was declared entitled to an advance of £2OO, free of interett, for 14 years.

LATEST NEWS. Tr. Ullathorne' the Roman Catholic Bishop of Birming- ham, lies seriously ill at Oscott College. On Thursday night, a party of armed and disguised men broke into the house of a man named Doherty, near Mohill, and stole some arms.

In view of the autumn session of Parliament, two COR- servative whips have already been sent out. Pairs are not longer to remain in force. It is stated that the Manchester Regiment and the Sea- forth Highlanders, upon their return from Egypt, will be quartered in Portsmouth garrison. At Portsmouth, on Thursday, an old woman, who had been previously convicted one hundred and sixty-four times was sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment for being drunk and disorderly. According to latest arrangements, the Queen and Princess Beatrice will leave Balmoral on November 16th, arriving at Windsor Castle about nine o'clock on the following morning. The search for the bodies in the Dinas Pit, Glamorgan- shire, where 63 persons were killed three years since by an explosion, continues, and additional discoveries are expected within the next few days. There have been eight deaths from scarlet fever at Accrington during this week as compared with seyen last week, and making 42 fatal cases since the beginning of Sep- tember. The new outbreaks are not so numerous as they have been.

Dr. James Culross, minister of Adelaide Place Church, Glasgow, the largest Baptist congregation in Scotland, has received an invitation to become Principal of Bristol Bap- tist College, in succession to the Rev. Dr. Gotch. Dr. Culross has been four years in Glasgow.

div.head: RETURN OF TROOPS FROM EGYPT.
div.p: RETURN OF TROOPS FROM EGYPT.

According to information from the War Office, 14 of the hired transport vessels may be expected to arrive in Eng- land with troops from Egypt within a week of each other, and daring the ensuing fortnight, the Guards being ex- pected by Wednesday or Thursday next. Orders have been received at the Herbert Hospital, Woolwich, to prepare for the reception of a number of sick and wounded. The following announcement was made at the Admiralty last night :—" The Queen has signified her commands for the granting of a medal to all the forces, naval and military. . . .

engaged in the operations in Egypt; two clasps are also to be given, one with the words Alexandria, which is to be granted to those present on the 11th of July, 1852; the other clasp will be inscribed Tel-ei-Kebir." SIR THOMAS GLASTONE AND THE PREMIER. On Thursday, at a meeting of the Kincardineshire Con- servative Association, Mr. Sinclair said the adoption of Lord Beaconsfield's policy by Mr. Gladstone reminded him of the Prodigal Son, and the Premier might yet adopt the politics and return to the house of Gladstone. Sir Thomas Glad- stone, in reply, said if ever that most distingnished gentle- man did return, he should not want on his part a most hearty and affectionate reception.

div.head: ASSAULTING A NEWSPAPER PROPRIETOR.
div.p: ASSAULTING A NEWSPAPER PROPRIETOR.

At the Sheffield Quarter Sessions, yesterday, a case which excited the greatest interest came before the Recorder. The defendant, Mr. William Jackson, veterinary surgeon, was indicted for assaulting Mr. Murphy, proprietor of the Sheffield Post. The assault was committed in an hotel, and arose out of a series of personal articles which appeared in the prosecuter's paper, one of which was devoted to the defendant. He was found guilty, but was only fined £2O.

div.head: SUICIDE FROM NOTRE DIME.
div.p: THE SUICIDE FROM NOTRE DIME.

The girl Marie Felix, who threw herself from Notre Dame, Paris, has been admitted to funeral rites in the Cathedral, Dr. Brouardel, physician to the Morgue, having certified lesions in the brain, confirming the assertions of the relations that she had suicidal monomania.: s

div.head: CHARGE OF MURDER AGAINST A CHEMIST.
div.p: CHARGE OF MURDER AGAINST A CHEMIST.

The Potteries stipendiary at Stoke-on-Trent, yesterday morning, remanded William Hollis, chemist, on a charge of wilful murder. It was stated that last night prisoner administered a drug to a married woman, named Wood, who was living apart from her husband, and that she died almost immediately afterwards. Hollis was only a few months ago liberated on a ticket of leave, having been sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for a similar crime.

div.head: TREMENDOUS FLOODS IN THE MIDLANDS.
div.p: TREMENDOUS FLOODS IN THE MIDLANDS.

Floods of a very serious characted prevailed yesterday, in Warwickshire, Leicestershire, and other parts of the mid- land districts, consequent on the exceedingly heavy and continuous rainfall of the last two days. Vast tracks of land are wholly submerged, and in many places the course of:the rivers is completely hidden by the floods. In some of the country districts roads are impassible to pedestrians. THREATENED STRIKE IN THE CHAIN TRADE. The operatives engaged in the Staffordshire and Wor- cestershire dollied chain trade have resolved to give notice to-day (Saturday) for an advance in wages equiva- ltnt to ten per cent. It is contended that in consequence of improved trade the operatives are entitled to a sub- stantial advance in wages. A portion of the employers are unwilling to give the advance, and in the event of their persisting in refusing to comply a general strike will be declared.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY.

On Thursday night a shocking accident happened to a little boy named Joshua Fadries, four years of age, son of John Fadries, of the Eagle Inn. The child was play- ing in a yard at Stalybridge, belonging to Alderman Ives, near some flags, when one of them fell upon him and inflicted such severe injuaies that he was at once taken to Dr. Hopwood's surgery, and then taken home in an unconscious state, where he died about seven o'clock.
A GREAT WRECK.
APPALLING SCENE.

A Moscow journal gives an account of a collision between two passenger steamers on the Volga under mast extraor- dinary circumstances. It appears that the captain of one of the vessels, the Kachine, annoyed that his competitor, the Pok-,enig, obtained larger freights, resolved to run her do' 0. Ile chese the dark night of October 3rd for, his fi 'dish project, and, when near Makarey, overtook the ikoenig, and, despite the signals made by the captain, ran into her at full speed. The Pekoenig sank amid the shrieks of her passengers, while the Kachine, without lowering a boat er making the slightest effort to save the drowning wretches, steamed off. Some boats, howdver, put off from the shore, and the passengers and crew, with the exception of five, were rescued. THE DESRUCTION OF INGESTRE HALL.

The fire at Ingestre Hall, on Thursday, originated in the state dressing-room in the centre of the building by the overheating of a flue near which ran a main flooring beam. The Ingestre steam fire engine at first attempted to play on the fire, but meanwhile the flames crept along the hollow floors and wainscots and soon enveloped the whole building. About a third of the furniture and pictures had to be aban- doned, including the celebrated painting of the earl's grand- father, the popular Viceroy of Ireland. About midday the brigade rescued £5OO worth of plate, stored in the vault under the central hall. The door of the vault became nearly red hot. Reynold's portrait of Charlotte Talbot was also saved. A costly marble fireplace with carved columns was destroyed. Towards night a large portion of the east wing fell near the firemen, who, however, miraculously escaped.

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES The Classes will commence Monday next, October 9th, 1882. SYLLABUS i—Mondays : Practical Chemistry, 6-30 p.m. to 8-0 p.m.; Alkali Manufacture. 8-0 p.m. to 9 0 p.m. Tuesdays: Art-Drawing, 7-0 p.m. to 8-0 p.m.; Machine Construction and Drawing, 8-0 p.m. to 9-0 p.m. Wednesdays: Art-Drawing, 7-0 p.m, to 8-0 p.m.; Building Construction and Drawing, 8 0 pm. to 9-0 p.m. Thursdays: Inorganic Chemistry (Elemen- tary Stage) 7-0 p.m. to 8 0 p.m.: Inorganic Chemistry (Ad- vanced Stage), 8-0 p m. to 9-0 p.m. Fee, 3s. per Class for all Classes, except Practical Chemistry. Fee for Practical Chemistry 8s . and a deposit of ss. for the use of apparatus. This deposit will be returned at the end of the Session If breakages, &c., a:e made good. The Laboratory is now being fitted up in the most complete manner. Each Student will have a separate bench with lock- up cupboard allotted to him, and he will have full control and charge of the apparatus and re-agents. At the end of each lesson each student must put away the apparatus and re-agents in the lock-up cupboard. Should a Student lose his key be will be charged Is. for a new one. As the number of benches is limited, it is desirable that intending students should make application at once. If there are more applicants than benches, the Committee reserve to themselves the right of deciding which students are to have the preference. The Library will be open on Sundays from 6 until 9 p.m. J. MORRISON, Hon. Sec.

LOCAL BOARD FOR THE DISTRICT OF HAY- DOCK.—This is to GIVE NOTICE, that on FRIDAY. the 3rd day of NOVEMBER. 1882, at the Local Board Offices. Hay- dock, at 11 o'clock in the forenoon, there will be an AUDIT of the ACCOUNTS of the LOCAL BOARD for the District of Haydock, under and according to the provisions of,"The Public Health Act,.1875," and that a copy of the accounts to be audited, together with all rate books, account books, deeds, contracts, accounts, bills, vouchers, and receipts mentioned or referred to in such accounts, will be deposited in the offices of the said Local Board, and be open during office hours thereat, to the inspection of all persons interested, for seven days before the said audit and examination, and all such persons shall be at liberty to take copies of, or extracts from, the same without fee or reward.—Given this 10th day of October, 1882. THOMAS TURNBULL, Clerk to the Local Board for the District of ligiydock.
